﴿It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He might test you [as to] which of you is best in deed. But if you, [O Muhammad], say, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾:

The Noble Qur'an has addressed the matter of the creation of the earth and the heavens more than once.

We have said before: The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, willed to create the earth and the heavens in six days of worldly days, and it was possible for Him to create them in less than the blink of an eye by the word "Be" (kun). We also know that there is a difference between bringing a thing into existence and setting out the components of bringing a thing into existence.

An example of this, and to God belongs the highest likeness, is when a person wants to make "yogurt" (zabadi). He puts a portion of yogurt material, called "khamira" (starter culture), into an appropriate quantity of warm milk. This process takes the person only a few minutes. Then he leaves the milk mixed with the yogurt starter, and after twenty-four hours the milk mixed with the starter has actually turned into yogurt.

This happens with regard to human actions: they are actions that require treatment (time and process). But the actions of the Creator, glory be to Him, involve no treatment, because they all come about by the word "Be."

Or, as some scholars have said: God willed to make the creation of the earth and the heavens take six days. Some orientalists have taken from this verse, and from other verses, an opening for an attempt to undermine the Noble Qur'an, claiming that there is a contradiction in it. The Truth, glory be to Him, says here: ﴿It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days...﴾ [Hud]. They came to the verse of detail, gathered the days mentioned in it, and said: they are eight days. It is the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him: ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days and attribute to Him equals? That is the Lord of the worlds. And He placed firmly set mountains upon it, and blessed it, and determined therein its sustenance in four days, complete for those who ask. Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke and said to it and to the earth, "Come, willingly or by compulsion." They said, "We come willingly." So He completed them as seven heavens in two days...﴾ [Fussilat]. Here some orientalists said: If this were the story of the creation of the earth and the heavens, the verse of summary would not match the verse of detail.

One of them said: Suppose I have ten ardebs of wheat, and I give so-and-so five ardebs, and so-and-so three ardebs, and so-and-so I give two ardebs; and thus what I have is exhausted, because the detail matches the summary.

Some of these orientalists claimed that the detail is not equal to the summary. They did not realize that the speaker is God, glory be to Him, and that He is addressing people who possess the faculty of expression, clarity, eloquence and fluency; and these people understood what the orientalists did not understand.

They understood, as people of eloquence, that the Truth, glory be to Him, created the earth in two days, then placed in it firmly set mountains and blessed it, whether in the earth or in the mountains, and determined in it its sustenance; all of this is a continuation of the discussion about the earth.

An example of this: when I travel to Alexandria, I reach the city of Tanta in one hour, for instance, and Alexandria in two hours; that is, the hour of travel in which I reached Tanta is included within the two hours of travel to Alexandria.

Likewise, the creation of the earth, the firmly set mountains and the determination of sustenance, all of this occurred within four days, including the two days of the creation of the earth, and then the creation of the heaven came in two days.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And His Throne was upon the water...﴾ [Hud]. All these unseen matters have a fundamental proof, which is that the One who informed of them is the Truthful. No one doubts that the earth and the heavens are created, and no one doubts that the heavens and the earth are greater in creation than the creation of people; and there is no human being who has claimed that he created the earth or created the heavens.

We know the inventors of all human inventions, such as the electric lamp, the telephone, the microphone, the television, the car, and others.

But when we come to the heavens and the earth, we find no one who has claimed that he created them.

The Truth, glory be to Him, has informed us that He is the One who created them, and it stands as a claim for Him until an opponent appears; and this opponent will never appear.

All this creation is for the sake of trial: ﴿that He may test you [as to] which of you is best in deed...﴾ [Hud]. That is: that He may examine you as to which of you is best in deed. But who determines the deed? It is God, glory be to Him and exalted.

Does the Truth, glory be to Him, need to test His creatures?

No. God, glory be to Him, knows eternally all that will come from creation, but He, glory be to Him, desired by the testing that what comes from them should correspond to what He knew eternally, as a proof against them.

Thus the testing of the Truth, glory be to Him, for us is a testing of proof against us.

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿...But if you say, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾ [Hud]. Here the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, depicts the denial of the obstinate ones toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They throw words out carelessly, before these words pass through their thinking.

Had they passed these words through their thinking, it would have been logically impossible for them to say them.

The Messenger (ﷺ) informs them of the message of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, that they will be resurrected after death.

This is a statement of information that if they die, and they will certainly die, God, glory be to Him, will resurrect them. So what they said was only: ﴿...this is nothing but obvious magic.﴾ [Hud]. The news he tells them is news; so what is the place of magic in it? They know that he (ﷺ) said that only from the text of the Noble Qur'an, and they say of the Noble Qur'an that it is magic; so the text itself is from the magic by which they judged the Qur'an.

We explained before that the refutation of the issue of magic in the Qur'an has a logical proof alongside the saying; for if they claimed that the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or that Muhammad, in their understanding, had bewitched the people who followed him.

The sorcerer has an effect on the one bewitched, and the one bewitched has no part in the process of sorcery. So if Muhammad had bewitched the people who followed him, why did he not bewitch those who deny his message, in the same manner by which he bewitched others?

Since they have remained in their obstinacy toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ), this is evidence that the matter is not sorcery; for if it were so, he would have bewitched them all.

And their saying: ﴿...this is nothing but obvious magic.﴾ [Hud]: indicates that it is an all-encompassing magic, not magic for specific people; so the phrase ﴿obvious magic﴾ means: magic encompassing everyone whom he wishes to bewitch.

And the remaining of one person in disbelief without faith in the Messenger of God indicates that the matter is not sorcery.

1 The throne (al-'arsh) in language: the king's seat. God, glory be to Him, named the throne of the queen of Sheba a throne, saying: ﴿...and she has a great throne (23)﴾ [An-Naml]. The Throne of the Creator, glory be to Him, is not limited; the Lord of Honour mentioned it in His Book (21 times), attributed to Himself, glory be to Him.
2 Liyabluwakum (that He may test you): that He may examine you, and He is most knowing of your affair.
Ahsanu 'amala (best in deed): most obedient to God and most restrained from His prohibitions. [Kalimat al-Qur'an]
3 Nidd (equal): likeness and counterpart. Its plural is andad. God, exalted, said: ﴿So do not set up rivals to God (22)﴾ [Al-Baqara], that is, likenesses as partners. Exalted is God above what they say. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, adapted]
4 Rasa al-shay' yarsu rusuwwan: it became fixed and firm; and arsahu: he made it fixed and firm; and arsa al-safina: he moored the ship on the shore so that it does not move. The meaning of al-rawasi: the mountains, because they fix the earth so that it settles and does not tilt. God, exalted, said: ﴿And He cast into the earth firmly set mountains lest it shake with you (15)﴾ [An-Nahl], and God, exalted, said: ﴿And the mountains He set firmly (32)﴾ [An-Nazi'at]. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, adapted]
5 Aqwat: plural of qut, which is what sustains the vital spark of provision. In al-Sihah of al-Jawhari: it is what sustains the human body of food. [Lisan al-'Arab, entry: qwt]
6 ﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke...(11)﴾ [Fussilat]. Al-dukhan: the water vapour rising from it when the earth was created. Mentioned by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir [4/93].
7 "Qala fa-qadahunna" (He completed them): He created them. Qada here means creation. It is one of the words that come with many meanings, among which:
Completion: ﴿Then when you have completed your rites...(200)﴾ [Al-Baqara].
Command: ﴿And when He decrees a matter...(117)﴾ [Al-Baqara].
Covenant: ﴿When We conveyed to Moses the command...(44)﴾ [Al-Qasas].
Charge/injunction: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him...(23)﴾ [Al-Isra'].
8 Nafida-yanfadu nafadan wa nafadan: it perished, went away and was cut off, leaving nothing, from nafad, which is cessation. God, exalted, said: ﴿What is with you will end, and what is with God is enduring...(96)﴾ [An-Nahl].
9 Al-yawm (the day): in modern astronomy, the period of one rotation of the earth on its axis, lasting approximately twenty-four hours; its plural is ayyam. Ayyam al-'Arab: their battles. Ayyam Allah: days in which God's vengeance and punishment descended upon past disobedient nations, and His days in which He bestowed favour upon obedient righteous nations.
Yawm al-Din: the Day of Judgement. Yawm Hunayn: the day on which the battle of Hunayn took place. The day with God has a measure different from our day; sometimes it is a thousand years, and every star has its day, and every planet has its day. God, exalted, said: ﴿...And indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count (47)﴾ [Al-Hajj]. And it may be a measure of fifty thousand years, confirming His saying, exalted: ﴿...in a day whose extent is fifty thousand years (4)﴾ [Al-Ma'arij]. By this measure we understand the meaning of His saying, exalted, concerning the creation of the heavens and the earth: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens in two days...(12)﴾ [Fussilat]. God knows best the measure of these two days. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, adapted]
10 Therefore Abu Yahya Zakariyya al-Ansari said in his book "Fath al-Rahman bi-kashf ma yaltabis fi al-Qur'an," p. 373: "Two days: the creation of the earth is among the four days after them, and the meaning is within the completion of four days; and with the two days of the creation of the heavens they are six days. Sunday and Monday for the creation of the earth; Tuesday and Wednesday for the setting described in the verse and what follows it; Thursday and Friday for the creation of the heavens."
11 Balawtu al-shay' — aluwwu balwan wa bala'an: I tested it and examined it. God, exalted, said: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial (35)﴾ [Al-Anbiya'], that is, We test you with evil and with blessings, or with good and blessings, so that We may know the extent of your patience or gratitude, and the extent of your faith or disbelief. His saying, exalted: ﴿There every soul will know what it has sent forth (30)﴾ [Yunus], that is, it will know the reality of the deed it sent ahead, as the examiner knows the thing he examines. His saying, exalted: ﴿...and We will test your reports (31)﴾ [Muhammad], that is, We will know their truth from their falsehood. Among the purposes of trial and testing is the manifestation of the reality of the deed and the distinction between the good deed and other than it, as a preparation for reward or punishment. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, adapted]
12 It is reported that Abdullah ibn Umar said that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Which of you is best in deed...(7)﴾ [Hud], and said: "Which of you is best in intellect, most restrained from the prohibitions of God, and swiftest in obedience to God." Cited by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (4/3327) and al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (4/404), who attributed it to Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim in al-Tarikh and Ibn Mardawayh, in similar wording.
13 Alqa al-kalam 'ala 'awahinih (he threw out speech carelessly): he did not reflect upon it. It is said: if he is not concerned, he may be right or wrong; it is said: if he is negligent with it. Ibn al-Athir said: al-'awahin is to take a path other than the proper one in walking or speech, plural of 'ahina. 'Ahana al-shay': he let speech go as it came to him, hastily, whether wrong or right; that is, not reflecting upon speech before uttering it, and throwing it out as it is. [Lisan al-'Arab, root ʿ-h-n, adapted]

Al-Sha'rawi, Commentary on surah 11, verse 8 (part 1 of 2):

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says:

﴿And if We defer the punishment from them until a counted nation, they will surely say, "What is holding it back?" Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them, and there will befall them what they used to mock.﴾ (8)

Note this: the first lam in ﴿لئن﴾ after the "و" (wa) has come to indicate that the statement contains an emphatic oath, even though the oath is omitted. The lam has taken the place of the oath, and its full form is "والله لئن" (by Allah, if...).

An oath is used to emphasise what is sworn to by means of what is sworn by. Emphasising the sworn matter only comes where someone doubts it. You would not swear to a person you meet and say, "By Allah, you were at so-and-so's yesterday."

So the oath comes because of a doubt that has arisen in the listener's mind, and you do not swear at the outset.

The oath is used in proportion to the levels of doubt, and its particles serve to reinforce it.

The Noble Qur'an says here: ﴿And if We defer the punishment from them until a counted nation...﴾ (8).

The wa here is the wa of oath, and there is also a condition here. An oath requires an answer, and a condition also requires an answer.

When a condition and an oath come together, the eloquence of the style suffices with one answer, as when we say, "By Allah, if you do such-and-such, I will certainly do such-and-such with you."

Thus the answer of the oath stands in for the answer of the condition. Whichever comes first, whether it is the oath or the condition, is the one whose answer serves for the other.

As we say, "By Allah, if so-and-so comes, I will honour him." Here the oath comes first, and its answer serves in place of the answer of the condition. But if you say, "If so-and-so comes to you, by Allah, you will honour him," here the condition is the one that comes first. The two are alike, but the most that can be said is that the oath is emphasis and the condition is establishment (taʾsis, introducing new information). So if something with a predicate comes before both of them, both the condition and the oath, we give the answer of the condition immediately, as when we say, "Zayd, by Allah, if he comes to you, honour him." This is because the condition, as we said, is establishment and the oath is emphasis, and the condition takes precedence here, since establishment is more important than emphasis.

Here the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿And if We defer the punishment from them until a counted nation, they will surely say, "What is holding it back?"﴾ (8). The answer here belongs to the oath, and it stands in for the answer of the condition. That is: the punishment is deferred.

Allah, glorified is He, had threatened those who disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) that He would punish them. The punishment for the earlier nations was the punishment of annihilation. Upon some of them Allah sent a violent wind, some were seized by the Cry, some He drowned, and some the earth swallowed.

The task of the earlier messengers was to convey the message, and then the heavens would take charge of disciplining those who disbelieved in the messages.

But Allah, the Most High, willed to favour the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) over all the nations, and to have the disbelievers punished through battles.

When the Messenger (ﷺ) threatens them with punishment, punishment has a time of appearance. It may be delayed so that those around the disbelievers may see the misguidance and corruption. When Allah's punishment falls upon these disbelievers, no one will grieve over them.

Thus Allah willed respite and reprieve (al-imlaʾ), so that they would have a clear meaning in life. Reprieve is for the wrongdoer, so that his injustices increase to such a degree that the nation in which he lives comes to hate his oppression. Then, when punishment falls upon him, no one will show him compassion.

We know that the human soul is the child of what it witnesses. When a person kills and years pass over his case, then the sentence of execution is passed, people forget the sting of the first killing and feel compassion for the killer when the sentence of execution is issued.

That is why I always say: among the causes of the continuation of crimes is the slowness of trials, slowness which makes people's sympathies lie with the criminal, because the image of the victim has first disappeared from their memory.

But if people, at the time of punishment, were to recall the circumstances of the crime, they would rejoice at the sentence of death on the killer.

Likewise we find that the Truthful, glorified is He, when He wishes to punish someone, says: ﴿...and let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ (An-Nur, 2). This is so that the punishment takes place before the society that suffered from their corruption and suffered from their injustices. Whoever is assaulted in his honour and sees the punishment of the assailant is healed.

Here Allah, the Most High, makes clear to His Messenger (ﷺ): You had threatened them with punishment. We conceal the punishment by granting them respite, but they made this the object of ridicule, mockery and derision, and they asked, "Where is the punishment?"

We find the Qur'an saying on their tongues: ﴿And they said, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qiṭṭ) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ (Sad, 16). Al-qiṭṭ is the recompense for deeds, and it derives from qaṭṭ, meaning cutting.

Punishment is proportionate to the crime. If the crime is great, the punishment is great; if the crime is small, the punishment is limited. So the punishment matches the crime.

It is strange that some of them said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment.﴾ (Al-Anfal, 32).

And there came from their tongues what the Noble Qur'an quoted of their saying: ﴿Or You make the sky fall upon us in pieces (kisafan) as you claim.﴾ (Al-Isra, 92). There is no doubt that a person does not wish or hope that punishment should fall upon him, but they said this in defiance, scorn and mockery.

Allah, the Most High, willed not to punish the disbelievers who were contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as He had punished the disbelievers who were contemporaries of the earlier messages. This is because the Truthful, glorified is He, is the one who said: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them.﴾ (Al-Anfal, 33).

Besides this, there were people among them who concealed their faith, because they did not have the strength to confront the disbelievers, nor the means to migrate to the abode of faith, and their circumstances obliged them to live among the disbelievers.

There is something in surah al-Fath that clarifies this, when the Truthful, glorified is He, said: ﴿They are those who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and the offering held back from reaching its place of sacrifice. And were it not for believing men and believing women whom you did not know, that you might trample them and there would befall you from them guilt without knowledge—that Allah may admit into His mercy whom He wills. If they had been separated, We would have punished those who disbelieved among them with a painful punishment.﴾ (Al-Fath, 25). That is: if the disbelievers had been distinguished from the believers, Allah, the Most High, would have sent the painful punishment upon the disbelievers. But if the Muslims with their army, which was at Hudaybiyyah, had entered Makkah and a battle had taken place there, that battle would have struck all the people of Makkah, including the believers scattered among the disbelievers, who were not segregated to one side so that the Muslims could direct the blow at the disbelieving side.

Thus, if the fighting Muslims had struck, they would have struck some of the believers, and this is what the Truthful, glorified is He, does not want.

Here the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿And if We defer the punishment from them until a counted nation...﴾ (8). The nation (ummah) is a group or community of one kind, such as the nation of humankind, the nation of jinn, the nation of ants, and other creatures of Allah.

The Truthful, glorified is He, is the one who said: ﴿There is no creature on the earth, nor bird that flies with its wings, but they are communities like you. We have not neglected anything in the Book. Then unto their Lord they will be gathered.﴾ (Al-An'am, 38). The ummah is a group united by one system and one law, whose members are equal in everything, so each of these groups is an ummah. There is also the ummah in the sense of a period of time, as in the words of the Truthful, glorified is He: ﴿And the one who was saved of the two of them said, having remembered after a period (ummah)...﴾ (Yusuf, 45). That is: this man remembered after a period of time, and the period called "ummah" may be the time that bears one generation.

The ummah, then, is a community and group with a kind that unites it, with individual distinctions, and it meets in a general meaning.

The ummah of humankind is a rational, speaking animal. There is a general measure common to every human being, but there are differences in talents.

No human soul possesses the talent for engineering, medicine, commerce, pharmacy and accounting all together, because each of these trades requires study.

No person has a lifespan sufficient to specialise in all these fields. That is why each individual specialises in one field, to serve others in it, while others specialise in another field and serve the rest, and so on.

In this there is social solidarity, in which each individual feels that he needs others, and that he cannot live independent of all creation.

If one person knew all the trades in the world, of medicine, engineering, judgeship, plumbing, carpentry, agriculture and others, would he then have no need of the rest?

Therefore Allah, glorified is He, willed that societies be bound together out of necessity and compulsion, not out of favour from one to another.

The one who sweeps the street or works in cleaning the sewage does not do so as a favour. Rather he does it out of need, because he needs work and provision, because his body needs food and clothing to cover it, and his children ask for food, shelter and clothing. Were it not for this, he would not work at that trade.

If he is sincere in his work, Allah, glorified is He, makes him beloved of it, and even if his circumstances improve, he remains in this work, because he has fallen in love with perfecting his craft.

I once saw a man who worked in this trade, carrying the filth on his shoulder. When Allah widened his means, he bought a cart pulled by a donkey, to carry in it what he drained from those sewers.

When Allah widened his means still further, he bought a car fitted with a suction machine for filth, and he sat on the seat and operated the motor that pumped the sewage into the tank of the car set aside for that purpose.

Thus the ties of society must arise from need, not from favour, because favour carries no obligation to work, whereas need is what carries the obligation to work, so that the movement of life may proceed.

Whoever loves his work in whatever condition, Allah, the Most High, grants him success in it more, because he has respected the decree of Allah in himself, and did not disdain it. Allah, glorified is He, gives him all good from this work in proportion to his love for the work and his sincerity in it.

If you look at the great people in every trade, however humble it may be, you will find that their history began with their acceptance of the decree of Allah, glorified is He, concerning them.

We know that the worth of every person lies in what he does well. That is why you find the nation composed of complementary talents, not identical ones, so that each person needs the work of others.

That is why the Truthful, glorified is He, said: ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees, so that some of them may take others in service (sukhriyyan)...﴾ (Az-Zukhruf, 32). Because no one makes another serve him in work unless the one being served is in need of that work.

That is why you find someone who knocks on your door and asks: "Do you not need a driver? Do you not need a servant?"

The one in need is the one who offers himself, perhaps he will find the work he does well.

That is why the people of any person should not imagine that when he serves in any trade, he is serving the one he serves. No; he is serving his own need.

Thus the nation is bound together by a bond of needs, not a bond of favour.

The Truthful, glorified is He, said of our master Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation (ummah)...﴾ (An-Nahl, 120). This is because many talents were gathered in him, talents that gather only in a whole nation of people.

The word "ummah" is applied to a period of time, to a group of every kind, and to a man who combines all the virtues of goodness.

Here the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿And if We defer the punishment from them until a counted nation...﴾ (8). The phrase "counted" (maʿdudah) usually comes to indicate fewness, as in the words of the Truthful, glorified is He: ﴿And they sold him for a paltry price, a few counted dirhams, and they were of those who had no desire for him.﴾ (Yusuf, 20). Since the price was paltry, the dirhams must be counted.

The reason we understand that the word "counted" indicates fewness is that we do not undertake to count a thing except when we suppose we are able to count it, because it is few. What we do not undertake to count is the abundant.

An example of this: no one has counted the sand or the stars.

That is why the words of the Truthful, glorified is He, came: ﴿And if you tried to count the favours of Allah, you could not enumerate them.﴾ (Ibrahim, 34). And "in" (inna), as we know, comes to express doubt, and the favours of Allah...

1 Al-ummah: a shared term, used in eight senses.
1. The ummah is a community (jamaʿah), as in His words: ﴿...and he found around it a community of people...﴾ (Al-Qasas, 23).
2. The ummah: the followers of the prophets, peace be upon them.
3. The ummah: a man who combines goodness and is followed as an example, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was a nation, devoutly obedient to Allah, upright...﴾ (An-Nahl, 120).
4. The ummah: religion and creed, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion (ummah)...﴾ (Az-Zukhruf, 22).
5. The ummah: a period and an age, as in His words: ﴿And if We defer the punishment from them until a counted nation...﴾ (Hud, 8).
6. The ummah: stature, meaning a person's height and tallness.
7. The ummah: a man who stands alone in his religion, with no one sharing it with him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl will be raised as an ummah on his own."
8. The ummah: the mother. It is said: "This is the ummah of Zayd," meaning the mother of Zayd.
[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi (4/3327) and Lisan al-ʿArab.]

2 Ummah maʿdudah: until a counted term, that is, a specified appointed time. The ummah in this place means the term and the period. The Most High said in surah Yusuf: ﴿And the one who was saved of the two of them said, having remembered after a period, "I will inform you of its interpretation..."﴾ (Yusuf, 45).

3 Yahbisuhu: holds it back, prevents it.

4 Haqqa bihim: befell them, and encompassed them. The Most High said: ﴿...and there befell the people of Pharaoh the evil of punishment﴾ (Ghafir, 45). [Abridged Tafsir al-Tabari, with adaptation.]

5 Tara al-shakk: a doubt arose and occurred in the mind of the listener, which requires the speaker to swear to what he says so that the listener will believe him.

6 The Most High said: ﴿So each We seized for his sin. Among them were those upon whom We sent a storm of pebbles, and among them were those seized by the Cry, and among them were those whom We caused the earth to swallow, and among them were those whom We drowned. And Allah would not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ (Al-ʿAnkabut, 40). As for those punished by the hasib, which is the fierce, extremely cold wind carrying the pebbles of the earth, they were the people of ʿAd. As for Thamud, they were seized by the Cry. The one punished by being swallowed was Qarun. The one punished by drowning was Pharaoh, his minister Haman, and their armies.

7 Al-imla': deferral and respite. The Most High said: ﴿And I give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ (Al-A'raf, 183). [Al-Mu'jam al-Wasit, with adaptation.]

8 From Abu Musa (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, gives respite to the wrongdoer, until when He seizes him, He does not let him go." Then he recited: ﴿And thus is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are wrongdoers. Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe.﴾ (Hud, 102). Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (4686) and Muslim (2583), in the Book of Righteousness and Kinship.

9 Ta'ifah: a group. It is said: three. It is said: four, the number of witnesses to adultery. The punishment in this noble verse means the prescribed penalty for fornication by an unmarried person. The rest of the verse is: ﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterer, lash each one of them with a hundred lashes, and let not pity for them take you in the religion of Allah, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. And let a group of the believers witness their punishment.﴾ (An-Nur, 2). [Tafsir al-Jalalayn, with adaptation.]

10 Qitta: that is, our share of the punishment He promised. [Kalimat al-Qur'an by Shaykh Muhammad Makhluf.] Qatta al-shay' and qattatahu: he cut it.

11 Kisafan: pieces. [Abridged Tafsir al-Tabari and Kalimat al-Qur'an.] Al-kisfah (with a kasra and sukun on the sin, and a fatha on the fa'): a piece of a thing. Its plural is kisaf and kusf. It has been read kisafan with a fatha on the sin, and also with a sukun.

12 Al-mujabahah: confrontation and rebuttal of opponents. Jabahahu: he struck his forehead, or confronted him with what he disliked, or turned him away from his need.

13 Al-hady: the camels that the Messenger (ﷺ) brought to the sanctuary, and it is one of the rites of pilgrimage. Ma'kufan: held back and prevented from reaching the place of sacrifice, which is the sanctuary. [Tafsir al-Jalalayn and Kalimat al-Qur'an, with adaptation.]

14 Tuti'uhum: you destroy them along with the disbelievers.

15 Ma'arrah: something disliked, hardship, or disgrace.

16 Tazayyalu: be distinguished from the disbelievers in Makkah. [Kalimat al-Qur'an, Shaykh Makhluf.]

17 For this reason the Most High said: ﴿O you who believe, when you go forth in the cause of Allah, investigate carefully, and do not say to one who gives you the greeting of peace, "You are not a believer," seeking the goods of worldly life. For with Allah are abundant spoils. Thus you were before, and Allah conferred favour upon you, so investigate carefully. Indeed Allah is ever, of what you do, Acquainted.﴾ (An-Nisa', 94).

And among the occasions of revelation of this verse: al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad killed a Bedouin who said, "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "A believing man used to conceal his faith among a disbelieving people, then he revealed his faith, and you killed him. Likewise, you used to conceal your faith in Makkah before." Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir (exegesis) (1/94) and attributed it to al-Bazzar. al-Suyuti, in al-Durr al-Manthur (2/644), attributed it to al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad and to al-Tabarani, from a hadith of Ibn Abbas.

18 ﴿ما فرطنا﴾ (We have neglected nothing): meaning that their knowledge is all with Allah, and He does not forget any one of them in respect of their provision and His management, whether it is on land or at sea. Ibn Kathir said this in his tafsir (2/131).

19 ﴿جرم اذكر﴾: its original form is اذتكر (idhtakar), on the pattern of افتعل (ifta'ala). The ت of the infix was changed to د, and the ذ of the verb was changed to د, and the two dals were assimilated. Compare the Qur'anic words: ﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ [al-Qamar 17].

20 الاستنكاف (al-istinkaf): arrogance, refusal, and being taken by disdain to do something. Compare the Qur'anic words: ﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor will the angels who are near [to Him]. And whoever disdains His worship and is arrogant - He will gather them to Himself, all of them﴾ [al-Nisa 172].

21 سخريا (sukhriyyan): made to serve in work, employed in it. [Kalimat al-Qur'an] That is, some of them employ one another in various tasks according to the skill each of them has in them. Allah the Exalted made this a means of livelihood in this world, so that people are bound together and grow close, and each does not isolate himself far from others, for life would then be corrupted.

22 Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (رضي الله عنه) was asked about the word الأمة (ummah) in the verse ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation devoutly obedient to Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 120]. He said: "The ummah is the teacher of good, and the qanit is the one who is obedient to Allah." Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his tafsir (2/590).

23 أمة معدودة (ummatin ma'dudah): a group of days, few in number. [Kalimat al-Qur'an]

24 شروه (sharawhu): they sold him. It was said: they were the caravan (al-sayyarah), who bargained with Yusuf (peace be upon him) for a price of بخس (bakhs): little. It was also said: it was unlawful, because it was forbidden for them, and it was not lawful for them to eat its price. ﴿And they were of those who were uninterested in him﴾: it was said they were the caravan, who were uninterested in him, not knowing his nobility with Allah and his prophethood. [Mukhtasar Tafsir al-Tabari]

The two Jalals mentioned in their tafsir that بخس means deficient, and that the counted dirhams were twenty or twenty-two dirhams, and that his brothers were the ones who were uninterested in him. The caravan that bought him brought him to Egypt, and the one who bought him sold him for twenty dinars, two pairs of sandals, and two garments. [Tafsir al-Jalalayn] with adaptation.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 11, verse 9:

The Truthful (al-Haqq), glory be to Him, says after that:

﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us, then withdraw it from him, indeed he is despairing and ungrateful.(1)(9)﴾

Here too the noble verse begins with His words: ﴿And if (wa-la'in)﴾. This means that the lam has preceded it to indicate an oath, as if He is saying: "If We let man taste mercy, then withdraw it from him, he would fall into despair." Here too there is an oath and a condition, and the oath precedes, so the response belongs to the oath.

The word ﴿We let (adhaqna)﴾ makes clear that the primary location of tasting (idhaqa) is the mouth, and its meaning is: taking a thing in order to perceive its taste, sweet or bitter, pungent or not pungent, alkaline or sour.

Among the marvels of the precision of human creation is that each region of the tongue has a taste to which it responds: the tip of the tongue responds to one particular taste, the middle of the tongue responds to another taste, the sides of the tongue respond to a third taste, and so on. All of this is in one organ, which the Truthful, glory be to Him, willed with this precision of composition.

Every "papilla" (halama) among the components of the tongue has something it senses; for this reason you find a person tasting food and saying: "The food lacks salt," or tasting a sweet, such as kunafa, and saying: "The sugar with which it is sweetened is precisely measured."

Likewise the body's temperature: a person measures his temperature, and if he finds it thirty-seven and a half degrees, he says: "It is a normal temperature." If a person's temperature falls below that, it is said: "He is suffering from hypothermia (al-hubut)." If it rises, it is said: "He is suffering from fever (al-hummá)."

This is a measure of the temperature of the human body as a whole, and it has its own specific outlets. But every organ in the body requires a specific temperature of its own in order to perform its work.

So the liver, if its temperature falls below forty degrees, does not perform its task. The human body contains many organs; the temperature of the eye, for example, is nine degrees; if its temperature rose above that, the eye would burst. The temperature of the ear is eight degrees.

You cannot bring together things of different temperatures and place them with one another, but the Truthful, glory be to Him and exalted, willed that for the human body.

Here the Truthful, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And if We let man taste...(9)﴾ [Hud]. Tasting (dhawq) is for perception, not for eating. When you buy fruit, the seller says to you: "Please, taste," and you take one of them to find out its flavour. Tasting, then, is taking a thing in order to perceive its taste.

When the Truthful, glory be to Him and exalted, wills that a blessing (ni'mah)(3) befall a person and then be taken from him, the person is afflicted with anxiety, sorrow, panic, or despair.

Whatever the blessing's smallness, a person enjoys it, and if it is withdrawn from him, he is despairing and ungrateful.

Despair (al-yas) is cutting off hope of something occurring. Because man does not possess the action, and if he were able to do it he would not despair. The believer never despairs, because God, glory be to Him, is the One who said: ﴿...Indeed, none despairs of the mercy (rawh)(4) of God except the disbelieving people(87)﴾ [Yusuf]. Despair, then, is that you cut off hope in a matter you desire, and you do not possess the means to achieve it.

The one who despairs is the one who has no God to rely upon, for God, the Exalted, is the Firm, Rightly-guided Support. If the believer loses something, he says: "God will compensate me with something better than it."

As for one who has no faith in a god, he says: "This chance may not recur another time."

A man from whom a pound is stolen may grieve, but if he has ten pounds at home, he grieves a little over the lost pound.

A person does not despair except when he is not certain of a source that will return to him what he wants; but when he believes in a source that will return to him what he wants, you will not find him despairing or hopeless.

The believer knows that a blessing has a Giver: if it comes, he thanks God for it, and if it is taken from him, he knows that the Truthful, glory be to Him, has taken it for a wisdom(5).

The Truthful, glory be to Him, says here: ﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us...(9)﴾ [Hud]. We know that "man" is meant to include all the children of Adam, peace be upon him, and they are many, among them the believer and the disbeliever.

Here the word "man" comes in its general sense, but the Truthful, glory be to Him, makes an exception for the believer in another place, when the Truthful, glory be to Him, says: ﴿By time(1), indeed man is in loss(2), except those who believe...(3)﴾ [al-'Asr]. "Man" is singular and denotes man in all its meanings, and from the kind of man is excepted whoever believes in Him.

So if you see the word insan (man), know that what is meant by it is all individuals of mankind.

If man isolates himself from the method of God, the Exalted, he is in loss, unless he follows the method of God; the method protects him from slipping, and his instincts proceed to what the Truthful, glory be to Him, intended for them.

God, glory be to Him, created the instincts for essential purposes: the instinct of hunger makes man seek food, and thirst was willed by God, glory be to Him and exalted, so that man would attend to seeking to quench himself with water.

The instinct for the preservation of the species drives man to marriage, and the instinct of curiosity is what drives man to uncover inventions.

The Truthful, glory be to Him, is the One who said of those who are heedless of exploring the signs of God, the Exalted:

﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth do they pass by, while they turn away from it?(105)﴾ [Yusuf]. The scientific, experimental, laboratory researcher examines the phenomena of the universe in order to discover the secrets of the universe.

There is a difference between curiosity for discovering the secrets of the universe and curiosity for the news of people.

Curiosity in general is the axis of the encounters of the universe, but religion and ethics are what guide curiosity.

So, the instincts have a function that must not slip into other than it, and religion has come to elevate the instincts and direct them to their functions.

For this reason you find the Truthful, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿And do not spy(8)...(12)﴾ [al-Hujurat]. That is: do not pursue the faults (awrat)(9) of people, for if we permitted one person to pursue people's faults, we would be permitting all others to pursue his faults.

When the Truthful, glory be to Him and exalted, prohibits man from pursuing the faults of others, He has protected him from others pursuing his faults.

Here the Truthful, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us, then withdraw it from him...(9)﴾ [Hud]. The word "withdrawal" (nazc) indicates that man is eager for what God, the Exalted, has granted him of goodness, health, well-being and ease. When the blessing is taken from him, he resists.

Withdrawal (nazc) means: the one from whom something is withdrawn holds firmly onto the thing withdrawn.

For this reason the Truthful, glory be to Him, says in Surat Ali 'Imran: ﴿Say: "O God, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You withdraw sovereignty from whom You will...(26)﴾ [Ali 'Imran]. The one who possesses sovereignty clings to it very tightly.

Here the Truthful, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us, then withdraw it(10) from him, indeed he is despairing and ungrateful(9)﴾ [Hud].

In the same surah the exception comes, and the Truthful, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Except those who are patient and do righteous deeds; those will have forgiveness and a great reward(11)﴾ [Hud].

We will come to its reflections after that.

In contrast to the one from whom mercy is withdrawn, and to the despairing ungrateful one, the Truthful, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And if We let him taste blessing (na'ma)(11) after adversity has touched him(12), he will surely say: "The evils (sayyi'at)(13) have gone from me," indeed he is exultant(14), boastful(15)(10)﴾

1 Ya'us (despairing): an intensive form from despair, meaning: he remains despairing and hopeless of God's mercy and goodness. Kafur (ungrateful): an intensive form from disbelief, meaning: little thankful for blessings; ingratitude for blessings is denying them and not thanking God for them. [Abridged Tafsir al-Tabari], adapted.
2 Perception occurs through the senses, and through perception emotional response occurs, and through emotion choice occurs; tasting is taking a thing in order to perceive its taste, whereby choice takes place.
3 Ni'ma (blessing) and ni'ma: the verb na'ima, he is comfortable, with the form from fariha, and it comes from the pattern karuma, ni'mah and ni'mah with the nun vowelled with fatha or kasra. Na'im: he was in ease of living and enjoyment of it. Al-na'im is what one takes pleasure in, of food, clothing and health. The Truthful says: ﴿...in the gardens of bliss(9)﴾ [Yunus], that is, those in which is every bliss. Al-ni'mah with fatha: bliss, and it applies to what a person enjoys of the means of luxury. The Truthful says: ﴿And leave me with the deniers, possessors of blessing...(11)﴾ [al-Muzzammil], in this world. Al-ni'mah with kasra: a verbal noun in the sense of bliss, and it is applied to the enjoyment and goodness that a person enjoys. The Truthful says: ﴿And if you count God's blessing, you cannot number it...(18)﴾ [al-Nahl]. Al-Qamus al-Qawim, adapted.
4 Rawh Allah (the spirit of God): His mercy, relief, and kindness to His servants in relieving their distress. [Words of the Qur'an], adapted. Despair is the cutting off of hope, and a person's hope in God, the Exalted, is not cut off unless he is a disbeliever.
5 On the authority of Suhayb al-Rumi, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "How wondrous is the affair of the believer! All his affairs are good, and this is not so for anyone except the believer: if prosperity befalls him, he gives thanks, and that is good for him; and if adversity befalls him, he endures patiently, and that is good for him." Related by Muslim in his Sahih (2999).
6 Khusr: destruction and deficiency.
7 Wa-ka'in: meaning "and how many." Ayah here: a lesson and a proof, like the sun, the moon, and other signs of God, the Exalted, which they see and witness but do not reflect upon. [Abridged Tafsir al-Tabari]
Abu al-Shaykh al-Isbahani related from al-Dahhak in explaining the meaning of the verse: that is, its sun, its moon, its stars, its clouds; and on the earth, what is in it of creatures, rivers, mountains, cities and palaces. Mentioned by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (4/593).
8 La tajassasu: that is, la tatajassasu, one of the two tas is dropped for a rhetorical purpose, and the meaning is: not pursuing people's faults and defects by searching for them. [Tafsir al-Jalalayn], adapted.
9 Awrah: what a person covers of his body out of modesty. Awrah also means a flaw or defect. A house is awrah, meaning it has a flaw. His words: ﴿They say: "Indeed our houses are exposed (awrah)..."(13)﴾ [al-Ahzab], meaning: it has a flaw through which enemies may fear to enter, so that they would turn back from jihad. Al-Qamus al-Qawim, briefly.
10 The intended meaning is the mercy with which God has blessed him.
11 Al-na'ma: the effect of blessing on the body and life of a person, so that it remains with him.
12 Al-darra': the effect of poverty and hardship. The Exalted says: ﴿And the patient in misfortune and adversity and in time of battle...(177)﴾ [al-Baqarah]. And the Exalted says: ﴿And We had certainly sent to nations before you, and We seized them with misfortune and adversity...(42)﴾ [al-An'am].
Massathu: afflicted him. [Tafsir al-Jalalayn and Abridged Tafsir al-Tabari], adapted.
13 Al-sayyi'at: calamities, hardships and difficulty.
14 Farih: an intensive form of farah, which is exultation over a blessing [Words of the Qur'an].
15 Fakhur: an intensive form of fakhr, meaning: much boasting of what one has gained among people, boasting over people of what has been given, and not thanking God, the Exalted, for His blessings. [Abridged Tafsir al-Tabari and Tafsir al-Jalalayn], adapted.

Here we find adversity (ḍarrāʾ) as the existing state, and ease (nuʿmāʾ) as the state that arrives, the reverse of the first case, where mercy, in the form of goodness and ease, was the existing state.

So the removal (of hardship) in the first case befell an existing mercy, while the ease befell an existing adversity.

There is a difference between naʿmāʾ and niʿmah, and between ḍarrāʾ and ḍurr. Ḍurr is that which pains the soul, while niʿmah is that which the soul enjoys.

Yet enjoyment and pain may exist within the soul without showing any trace upon the person. If the effect of blessing appears upon the person, it is called "naʿmāʾ"; if the effect of harm appears upon him, it is called "ḍarrāʾ".

Here the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And if We let him taste ease after hardship has touched him, he will surely say, "The evils have gone from me..."﴾ [Hud] (10). The one who says this does not perceive the path by which the evils departed, because an evil does not depart on its own.

Had the speaker been a believer, he would have said: "God has removed the evils from me." But he is not a believer; therefore he drowns in false joy and baseless pride.

The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, describes him with His words: ﴿...Indeed, he is exultant and boastful﴾ [Hud] (10). It is as though the joy in the blessing has distracted him (1) from the Bestower, and from the One who removed the evil from him.

As for pride (fakhr), we know that pride is self-regard for one's virtues (2), and you may find a person boasting over another by mentioning to him virtues and glories that the other does not possess.

We know that distinction of an individual exists within society, but the etiquette of faith requires that a person not boast of his distinction.

For this reason we find the Prophet (ﷺ) saying: "I am the master of the children of Adam on the Day of Resurrection, and I say so without pride" (3).

In one battle we find him (ﷺ) saying: "I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib" (4). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was compelled to say this because the disbelievers in that battle thought they had surrounded him and those with him, and that he would flee. But he (ﷺ), with his courage, declared: "I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib" (5), and he was the nearest of the Muslims to the position of the disbelieving enemies and facing them.

We find people who escalate or compete, one of them entering upon the other with a loud voice to shake the other party's confidence in himself.

The boastful person is one who is absent, veiled by heedlessness, from the Giver of the virtues he boasts of. Had he kept in mind the majesty of the Giver, he would have shrunk before Him; and had the insight of the arrogant and boastful turned to the Truth, glory be to Him, he would have shrunk before Him and returned every thing to the Giver.

An example of this in the Noble Qur'an is the words of the Truth, glory be to Him, on the tongue of the companion of Moses, peace be upon them both: ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord...﴾ [al-Kahf] (82). This is the conduct of the humble worshipper.

As for the state of the boastful who are heedless of the Truth, glory be to Him, the Qur'an portrays it in the words of Qarun: ﴿I was only given it on account of knowledge that I have...﴾ [al-Qasas] (78).

His end was the true statement: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his house...﴾ [al-Qasas] (81).

For this reason we have said: you protect every blessing you have by saying, when you see it, "Bismillah, mā shāʾ Allāh" (In the name of God; what God wills), so that you remember that this blessing did not come by your effort alone, but came to you first by the will of God, glory be to Him, so that the eye of the Bestower remains a guard over the blessing you possess.

But when you forget the Bestower, He will not preserve that blessing for you. We observe that the Truth, glory be to Him, has not forbidden the joy that springs from the expansion of the breast and the delight in God's blessing; rather He asked us for it in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿Say: "By the bounty of God and His mercy—in that let them rejoice"...﴾ [Yunus] (58).

However, the Truth requires of the believer that his joy not arise from the most trivial causes and cling to him, otherwise he would be among the exultant whom God has censured (9).

(1) Dhuhūl ʿan al-shayʾ (heedlessness of a thing): that another matter preoccupies you with it. Dhahila ʿan al-shayʾ: he left it deliberately, or neglected it, or forgot it due to preoccupation. [Lisān al-ʿArab, root dh-h-l].

(2) Manāqib: plural of manqabah, which is nobility of deed. Karīm al-manāqib: good character, noble conduct. [Lisān al-ʿArab], adapted.

(3) Narrated by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ (2278) and al-Bayhaqī in Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwah (5/476) from Abū Hurayrah. In al-Ḥākim's Mustadrak (2/604), which he declared authentic, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh with the wording: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say so without pride," without the mention of "on the Day of Resurrection."

(4) The Messenger of God (ﷺ) attributed himself to his grandfather ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib rather than to his father ʿAbd Allāh, for ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib was widely and openly famous, and was the chief of the people of Makkah. It was well known among them that ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib had been given good news of the Prophet (ﷺ), that he would appear and that his station would be great. The Prophet (ﷺ) wished to remind them of this and to alert them that he would certainly prevail over his enemies and that the final outcome belongs to him, in order to strengthen their souls. Transmitted by al-Nawawī in his commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (12/360).

(5) For a man asked al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib: "Did you flee from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Ḥunayn?" Al-Barāʾ replied: "But the Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not flee. The Hawāzin were archers that day, and when we charged against them they scattered, and we fell upon the spoils, and they met us with arrows. I saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on his white mule, and Abū Sufyān ibn al-Ḥārith was holding its bridle, and he was saying: 'I am the Prophet, no lie; I am the son of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.'"
Narrated by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ (1776), Kitāb al-Jihād, and al-Bukhārī in his Ṣaḥīḥ (4317), from al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib.

(6) The intended meaning is what al-Khiḍr (peace be upon him) did: tearing the boat, killing the boy, and rebuilding the wall that was about to collapse.

(7) Ūtītuhu: i.e., I acquired it. It refers to the wealth God had provided him, but Qarun claimed that his own knowledge had brought him the wealth, thereby denying God's blessing upon him, and so he deserved God's punishment.

(8) Khasf: God caused the earth to swallow (khasafa Allāh al-arḍ): made it sink and recede. The Truth says: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his house...﴾ [al-Qasas] (81). Khasaf al-qamar: its light diminished. The eclipse of the sun occurs at the end of the Arab lunar month, on the days of al-muḥāq, and its cause is the moon's passing between the earth and the sun, so that the moon screens the sun. If the screening is total it is khusūf; if partial it is kusūf. The Lisān states: khasf is the sinking of the earth with what is upon it, i.e., its swallowing of what is above it; khasafa Allāh bihi al-arḍ means He made it disappear into it. Summarized from al-Qāmūs al-Qawīm.

(9) He said of the people of Moses that they said to Qarun: ﴿...Do not exult; indeed God does not love the exultant﴾ [al-Qasas] (76), i.e., the insolent, arrogant ones who do not acknowledge God's blessing upon them. And the Exalted said: ﴿So that you may not grieve over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you...﴾ [al-Ḥadīd] (23).

Allah, the Exalted, says after that:

﴿Except those who are patient and do righteous deeds; for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ (11)

The word ﴿patient﴾ (sabaru)(1) here corresponds to the two matters mentioned in the two preceding verses. There is the withdrawal of mercy, and likewise there is "ease after hardship." Both states require patience, because each of us is subject to the events that pass over him, and he must be patient in recognizing the wisdom of the All-Powerful, glorified is He.

Allah, the Exalted, begins this verse with an exception, saying, ﴿Except those who are patient...﴾ (11) [Hud]. Were it not for this exception, the ruling issued in the two preceding verses would apply to all of mankind: a ruling of despair and disbelief, or of exultation and boasting without remembering the Bestower of blessings, glorified is He.

This exception, however, came to reassure those who are patient regarding what may afflict them in the matter of the call (to Islam), or what may afflict them personally. Such affliction is not from the disbelievers, but is by the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing.

Or it means that they are patient in refraining from the deeds of their fellow believers.

So, patience (sabr) means restraining the self so that it is content with a disliked matter that has befallen it.(2) Disliked matters have several sources, among them:

* A matter in which you have no opponent (ghareem)(3), such as illness, for example.

* Or a matter in which you do have an opponent, such as when something of yours is stolen or you are attacked. In this case you are preoccupied with the desire for revenge, and your soul is inflamed with the desire to get back at this opponent, more than it would be if there were no opponent. When a person falls ill, he has no opponent.

In the case of the desire for revenge, patience differs from patience in the case where there is no opponent.

For this reason, Allah, the Exalted, presented patience according to these stages. Our master Luqman says to his son: ﴿...And be patient over what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring resolve.﴾ (17) [Luqman].

In another place, Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed, that is of the matters requiring resolve.﴾ (43) [al-Shura]. In this verse there is the emphatic lam, to affirm that this matter requires strong resolve, because there is an opponent in it who arouses my anger.

When I see someone who struck me, insulted me, stole from me, or harmed me gravely, the matter here requires patience, strength, and resolve.

As for the first case, where there is no opponent, Allah, the Exalted, suffices with the noble saying: ﴿...And be patient over what befalls you...﴾ (17) [Luqman].

However, in the other verse He, glorified is He, added the lam to affirm resolve, and to add, in the case of an opponent, the seeking of forgiveness. He says: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed, that is of the matters requiring resolve.﴾ (43) [al-Shura]. Thus we find the exception, namely those who are patient in their various states.

Here Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿Except those who are patient and do righteous deeds...﴾ (11) [Hud]. Since patience is mentioned here, patience applies only to harm. But beware that the harm comes from your opponent in faith, or from your opponent outside of faith, diverting you from your activity in obedience to Allah, glorified is He. Patience does not mean that you suppress your anger and torment yourself with this suppression in a way that diverts you from your tasks in life. Rather, Allah, the Exalted, permits you to rid yourself of your rancor and hatred by living with faith, which lessens the intensity of anger.

To break the sharpness of rancor, Allah, the Exalted, has permitted you to retaliate against whoever has attacked you with the same as he did to you, because He, the Exalted, does not want you to remain in a state of boiling anger or oppression that prevents you from working. Rather, Allah, the Exalted, wants you to direct your energies toward performing your work.

Therefore, Allah, the Exalted, obliges you only by the ruling of justice, and He, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿So whoever has aggressed against you, then aggress against him in the same manner as he aggressed against you...﴾ (194) [al-Baqarah].

But there is one who is able to control himself, and therefore Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿...those who restrain anger and pardon people. And Allah loves the doers of good.﴾ (134) [Al ʻImran]. The meaning of restraining anger (kazm al-ghayz)(5) is that the anger exists, but its bearer does not move with a vengeful impulse. It is like when you say, "I stoppered the waterskin," because the one carrying the waterskin, if he did not close it, the water would escape from it. That is, he holds the water inside it.

Restraining anger is a level and a station that may not be entirely positive, because the anger still exists. Therefore there comes a higher stage, represented in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿...and those who pardon people. And Allah loves the doers of good.﴾ (134) [Al ʻImran]. That is, you remove the anger from your heart and show forgiveness.

So, you are here before three stages: that you return the aggression against you with its like. But equivalence in repelling aggression is something that cannot truly be achieved. Whoever slaps you once, how can you control the amount of pain in the slap you return to him?

What governs the response to aggression is anger, and anger does not measure the aggression by its equal, so the required justice is not achieved. For this reason, patience is better, confirming the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿...And if you are patient, it is better for those who are patient.﴾ (126) [al-Nahl]. If you increase the strength of your slap, you become an aggressor.

Perhaps we recall Shakespeare's play "The Merchant of Venice," whose hero is that Jewish merchant who lent a man money, and the loan contract stipulated that the Jew would cut off a pound(6) of the borrower's flesh if he was late in repayment.

The borrower was late in repayment, and the Jewish usurer wanted to cut off a pound of the borrower's flesh. The matter was brought before the judge, who was a wise man, and he wished to issue a ruling seeking justice. The judge said: There is no objection to your taking a pound of the man's flesh. Bring the knife, and cut one pound without any increase or decrease. For if you take more than that, we will take the excess from your own flesh with the same knife. Likewise, if you cut less than a pound, we will cut the shortfall from your flesh as a punishment for you.

The Jewish usurer hesitated, because the butcher, any butcher, cannot control his hand to cut a pound of exact weight. Sometimes he cuts more than the required weight, and sometimes less, and then he adds to or subtracts from the weight in each case.

The Jewish usurer withdrew and gave up his claim. What drove him to that was his inability to take the exact equivalent. Had he risen a little in his feelings, he would not have reached this ruling.

Allah, the Exalted, urges us to repel aggression with its like, and if we wish to rise higher, then let us restrain anger. And if we wish to rise even further, then let us remove anger from the heart, but from those who pardon people, so that we may attain the love of Allah, the Exalted, because He, the Exalted, says:

﴿...those who restrain anger and pardon people. And Allah loves the doers of good.﴾ (134) [Al ʻImran]. In this, the believer rises through the method of Allah, glorified is He, making the one who was wronged the one who does good.

When you want to explain Allah's love for the doers of good philosophically, logically, or economically, you will find the matter is correct, and Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿And let them pardon and overlook. Would you not like that Allah should forgive you?...﴾ (22) [al-Nur](9). So if your brother wrongs you with an evil deed, you may either return it with its like, or restrain anger, or rise to pardon. In that way you become one of the doers of good, because if you have committed an evil deed and you know that Allah, the Exalted, forgives it for you, will you not feel joy?

So, since you want Allah, the Exalted, to forgive your wrong before Him, why not pardon your brother's wrong against you?

The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Would you not like that Allah should forgive you?...﴾ (22) [al-Nur]. Here Allah, the Exalted, has addressed the matter from the standpoint of the soul, making the servant's pardon of another's evil a good deed. The servant's pardon has a price with Allah, the Exalted, because the servant will receive the forgiveness of Allah, the Exalted. Beyond that, you leave the punishment of the offender and retaliation against him to your Lord, and in surrendering the matter to Him there is rest.

If you exact retribution from the one who wronged you, your retribution is proportionate to your strength. But if you leave him to the power of Allah, the Exalted, that is more difficult and arduous, because you have left him to the power of the Most Powerful.

Thus the one who pardons the offender attains an elevated rank, because he has placed Allah, glorified is He, on his side.

There are those who say: How does religion command people to do good to those who wronged them?

They explain it as a command against the self.

We say: Doing good to the offender is a stage of elevation, and not a fundamental obligation(12), because Allah, the Exalted, has permitted us to repel aggression with its like, then urged the believer to restrain his anger, or to rise to pardon, and to reach doing good. All of these are elevations of certainty in Allah, the Exalted.

Look at yourself, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness, and He is exalted above every likeness. If you want to apply the matter to yourself, when you find one of your children has aggressed against his brother, your heart, your feelings, and your gentleness are with the one who was wronged.

And the one who says: How does the Law obligate me to do good to whoever wronged me?

We say to him: Remember the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri, may Allah be pleased with him(13): "Shall I not do good to one whom Allah has placed on my side?"

If the world applied this principle with certainty and sincerity, life on earth would become a hastened paradise: tolerance, whose foundation is nearness, and whose method is love.

And here, in the verse about which we are reflecting, Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Except those who are patient and do righteous deeds; for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ (11) [Hud].

If someone asks: And why do they attain forgiveness?

We say: Because they were patient and forgave. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, bestows forgiveness upon them from Himself, because He was patient with the wrongdoing and forgave the one who wronged. He must reward him, not with forgiveness only, but with a great reward as well(14).

---

(1) "Those who were patient" in the past tense, and "those who persevere" in the present and future, are the people of success, confirming the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, be patient and endure and remain stationed and fear Allah that you may be successful.﴾ (200) [Al ʻImran].

(2) Patience is also required when a blessing is withheld, as a test of the believer's faith. On the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, some of the Ansar asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he gave them. Then they asked him again, and he gave them, until what he had was exhausted. Then, when he had spent everything in his hand, he said to them: "Whatever good I have, I will not withhold from you. Whoever seeks to abstain from asking, Allah will keep him chaste; whoever seeks self-sufficiency, Allah will make him self-sufficient; and whoever seeks to be patient, Allah will grant him patience. No one has been given a gift better and more expansive than patience." Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (6470) and Muslim in his Sahih (1053), in the Book of Zakat.

(3) Al-ghareem: the creditor and the debtor. Its plural is ghurama'. The intended meaning here is: the opponent or the enemy. [Lisan al-Arab, al-Mu'jam al-Wasit], adapted.

(4) Patience is either patience in carrying out commands, patience in avoiding prohibitions, or patience in accepting what has been decreed. Whoever possesses all these stations is among the people of resolve. "The matters requiring resolve" are the obligations that are necessary because they are obligatory. [Tafsir al-Jalalayn].

(5) Al-kazimin al-ghayz: those who suppress their anger in their hearts. [Kalimat al-Qur'an].
It is related from Mu'adh ibn Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever restrains anger while able to act upon it, Allah, the Exalted, will call him before the heads of creation on the Day of Resurrection, until He gives him the choice of whichever of the wide-eyed maidens he wishes." Related by Ahmad in his Musnad (3/440), Abu Dawud in his Sunan (4777), and al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan (2493, 2021), who said: "Hasan gharib."

(6) Al-ratl: a measure by which something is weighed or measured, which varies from region to region. In Egypt it is twelve ounces, and an ounce is twelve dirhams. Its plural is arta'l. [al-Mu'jam al-Wasit].

(7) Al-hadd: urging and encouraging the doing of something. [Lisan al-Arab], adapted. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, he did not believe in Allah, the Great. And he did not urge the feeding of the needy.﴾ (33-34) [al-Haqqah].

(8) On the authority of Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever would be pleased that buildings be raised high for him and ranks be elevated for him, let him pardon one who wronged him, give to one who deprived him, and maintain ties with one who severed them." Related by al-Hakim in his Mustadrak (2/295) from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and he said: "Its chain is sound, but they did not record it." Al-Dhahabi said: "In it is Abu Umayya, whom al-Daraqutni declared weak, and Ishaq did not meet 'Ubada."

(9) Safaha 'an rajul: he turned away from him or pardoned him and did not hold him accountable for his sin. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿...But if you pardon and overlook and forgive, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (14) [al-Taghabun]. And Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿...Indeed, the Hour is coming, so forgive with gracious forgiveness.﴾ (85) [al-Hijr]. [Lisan al-Arab], adapted.

(10) The complete verse: ﴿And let not those of virtue and wealth among you swear not to give to the near of kin and the needy and the emigrants for the cause of Allah. And let them pardon and overlook. Would you not like that Allah should forgive you? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (22) [al-Nur].
This verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, who swore that he would no longer give his maternal cousin Mistah ibn Uthatha the support he had previously given him, because of what he said about 'A'isha along with others who spoke, which is the event known as the Slander (al-Ifk). Then Allah, glorified is He, revealed the verse. Abu Bakr said: "By Allah, I love that Allah should forgive me," so he resumed the support he had been giving Mistah and said: "I will never withdraw it from him." See Tafsir Ibn Kathir (3/275) and Asbab al-Nuzul by al-Wahidi (p. 185), al-Maktaba al-Thaqafiyya edition.

(11) Asa'a is'a'ah: to commit an evil act, the opposite of "ahsana" (to do well). "Asa'a al-'amal" means he did not do the work well. Al-musi' is the active participle of asa'a. Al-sayyi' is the ugly and reprehensible. Al-sayyi'ah is the feminine of sayyi' in the sense of ugly. Al-sau'ah is that which is ugly to display and should be concealed. [al-Qamus al-Qawim], briefly.

(12) Because obligation is a binding requirement, while pardon is from grace, and dealing with grace is an elevation.

(13) He is al-Hasan ibn Yasar al-Basri, Abu Sa'id, a Successor (tabi'i). He was the imam of the people of Basra and the scholar of the Muslim community in his time, and one of the scholarly jurists and ascetics. He was born in Medina in 21 AH, and grew up under the care of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. He used to visit the governors, commanding them and forbidding them. He settled in Basra and died there in 110 AH at the age of 90.

(14) Allah's forgiveness, in return for the servant's patience and his pardoning of the offender's wrong, is limited by the limits of human capacity. But Allah's forgiveness encompasses the generosity of the Generous and the pardon of the Wise, because His pardon is accompanied by a reward, and the great reward is from the Greatest, who is Allah, glorified is He.

Then He, glorified is He, says afterward:

﴿Perhaps you may leave out some of what is revealed to you, and your breast may be constricted by it, lest they say, "Why has no treasure been sent down to him, or an angel come with him?" You are only a warner, and God is Guardian over all things.(1) (12)﴾: Here the Truth, glorified is He, uses the interrogative form in His saying, ﴿Perhaps you may leave out some of what is revealed to you... (12)﴾ [Hud]. It is an interrogative in the sense of a prohibition.

To God belongs the highest example. You may say to your son, to urge him to diligence, "Perhaps you were pleased by the failure of so-and-so." The import (fahwa(2)) of this address is an interrogative in the sense of a prohibition, and it carries hope.

Here you find that the one who hopes is your Lord, glorified and exalted is He, who sent you with the call.

Therefore the saying of the Truth, glorified is He, comes to make clear: Let your breast not be constricted, O Messenger of God, by these obstinate people, who want to drive you out of your station, the station you constantly insist upon. You always affirm to them that you are a human being.(3) It was incumbent upon them that what they ask of you should match what you have acknowledged about yourself. You never said of yourself that you are a god, so that they should ask you for signs that contradict the laws (nawamis(4)). Rather, you are a conveyer of a message from God, exalted is He.

Beware lest your breast be constricted so that you fail to convey anything of what has been sent down to you, for the conveying is the proof against them. If your breast were constricted by them and you diminished the conveyance entrusted to you, [they would have an argument]. For whenever they are informed of a sign, they deny it. Know that God, glorified and exalted is He, will surely increase their punishment in proportion to what they denied.

The word "constricted" (ضائق, ḍā'iq(5)) is an active participle. It means that the one described by it is about to remain possessed of this attribute so that it becomes a constant trait of his. Yet it expresses a stage among the stages, just as we say, "So-and-so is a carpenter (najjār)," meaning he is able to carry out carpentry work once or a few times, but he does not practise this craft as a profession.

Likewise the word "constricted," ḍā'iq, expresses a stage and no more, on account of the excess of denial and what they demanded of the Messenger, peace be upon him, of things that go beyond the bounds of his humanity. Here they asked that a treasure be sent down to him.

The Truth, glorified is He, mentioned the matter of the treasure to show us the extent of the values of life they held. The highest of their values was concentrated in wealth. Therefore they wished that this Qur'an had been sent down to one of the rich, in confirmation of the saying of the Truth, glorified is He: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man of the two towns?" (31)﴾ [al-Zukhruf]. So their objection was not to the Qur'an itself but to the one upon whom it was sent down.

In the noble verse we are reflecting upon, they asked that a treasure be sent down to him, thinking that wealth would divert him, and those with him, from the call to God. They forgot that they had previously offered him rule (al-thawra(6)).

Thus it became clear to anyone to whom this matter is presented that the matter of the treasure does not occupy him, peace be upon him.

The "treasure" (kanz) linguistically means a thing gathered together. If an animal is full of flesh, it is said of it, "packed with meat (muktanizah lahman)." But the word "treasure" has come to refer to that which is the price of anything, namely gold.

Therefore the Truth, glorified is He, said: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of God, give them tidings of a painful punishment... (34)﴾ [al-Tawbah].

We know that there is a difference between direct sustenance and indirect sustenance. Direct sustenance is what you benefit from, food or drink. There is something that brings you indirect sustenance, but it does not replace the direct, continuous sustenance.(7)

If a man were in the desert with heaps of gold (qanatir muqantarah(8)) and found no food or water, what would the gold do for him? If another man offered him a loaf of bread and a drink of water in exchange for all the gold he owns, he would agree immediately. Here the valuation is not that a qintar of gold is the price of a loaf and a drink of water; rather, a qintar of gold here is the price of continued life and the necessity of need.

So the meaning of the word "treasure" (kanz) is hoarded gold and silver money. In our colloquial Egyptian it is called "money under the paving stone." But if the owner of this money pays God's right concerning what he has stored, it is not considered a treasure, because the condition for a treasure is that it be hidden. The zakat that is paid from stored wealth shows society that the owner of the wealth does not hide what he has.

Therefore the word "treasure" is applied only to gathered wealth from which God's right is withheld. If God's right is paid, the status of being a treasure is lifted from it, because the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿...And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of God, give them tidings of a painful punishment (34)﴾ [al-Tawbah]. From this noble saying we understand that whoever owns wealth and pays God's right in it is not considered a hoarder. When zakat apparently reduces the wealth, it pushes the person to invest this wealth well, so that he does not lose it over a period of forty years, since the zakat on wealth is two and a half percent. Therefore the owner of wealth tries to make it grow, and in doing so he creates an opportunity for one who has no means and is able to work, so that unemployment decreases.

You may be the owner of wealth but not understand the secrets of trade and industry, so you partner with one who understands trade or industry, and in this way you open the doors of employment for one who has no work and is able to manage work.

This is the will of the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, to make the complementarity of talents a source of growth and increase: the complementarity of the talent of means (wujd, money) and the talent of effort (juhd). Between wujd and juhd movement arises. The owner of wealth agrees with the man of effort on the proportions of profit according to supply and demand, because every exchange is subject to this principle, supply and demand. Such cooperation between the one who has means and the one who is able produces a commodity, and a commodity has no desire of its own. Rather, the owner of the commodity and the buyer of the commodity have desires. The owner wishes to sell at the highest price, and the buyer wishes to buy at the lowest price, but the commodity itself has no desire.

As long as supply and demand govern commodities, this is a balance in the scale of the economy.(9)
