(51) When he said to his father and his people, "What are these statues to which you are devoted?" (52) They said, "We found our fathers worshipping them." (53) He said, "You have certainly been, you and your fathers, in manifest error." (54) They said, "Have you brought us the truth, or are you of those who jest?" (55) He said, "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them, and I am of those who testify to that." (56)﴾ [al-Anbiya'].

This is the certain upbringing (al-tarbiyya al-yaqiniyya(17)) that the Truth, glory be to Him, intended for Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to teach us how faith is.

The people of Ibrahim worshipped gods other than Allah, but Ibrahim, peace be upon him, arrived at the worship of the One who created him and created the universe, the Maker who sets the law for the preservation of what He makes, glory be to Him and exalted.

Therefore we notice his saying: ﴿He who created me, and it is He who guides me (78)﴾ [al-Shu'ara']. He did not say, "He who created me guides me," because that would be a claim that would be contested, and people would set laws for themselves; so the Truth, glory be to Him, made clear that the One who created is the One who guides.

The Truth, glory be to Him, brought the word "huwa" (He) for exclusivity, so that creation does not share with its Creator in it. But in the matter which is not claimed, He did not bring the word "huwa," as in His saying: ﴿And who causes me to die and then gives me life (81)﴾ [al-Shu'ara']. What creatures have no share in is brought by the Qur'an without emphasis of the pronoun, but in the other matter He brings emphasis of the pronoun, as in His saying: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me (80)﴾ [al-Shu'ara'].

It may be said, "The physician is the one who cures me," but that is not real, because Allah, glory be to Him, is the One who places knowledge, and He is the One who created the disease and created the cure(18).

Then after that the Truth, glory be to Him, says in the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿And when Ibrahim was raising the foundations(19) of the House...﴾ (127) [al-Baqarah].

So, every occasion that comes to affirm a meaning of the meanings of faith comes with it a snapshot from the snapshots of the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and if you gather all the snapshots you will find the story of Ibrahim complete.

And if Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, wishes to relate the stories to His Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, that is to strengthen his heart, peace be upon him.

﴿And We relate to you the news of the messengers that We may strengthen thereby your heart...﴾ (120) [Hud]. Because the Prophet, peace be upon him, is exposed to many events, Allah reminds him of what happened to the messengers, peace be upon them, and brings the faith-building snapshots to strengthen the heart of the Messenger, peace be upon him.

And here the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿...They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace," and it was not long before he brought a roasted calf (69)﴾ [Hud].

In another place the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you." (52)﴾ [al-Hijr]. And in another verse the Truth, glory be to Him, speaks of this situation: ﴿So he sensed within himself a fear of them. They said, "Fear not," and gave him good tidings of a knowing boy. (28)﴾ [al-Dhariyat]. That is: he felt fear within himself, and this is a matter of al-mawajid (inner states); because every act has preliminaries that begin with perception, then inclination, then action. So when Ibrahim, peace be upon him, saw them, he sensed fear within himself, then inclined toward an act, which was the greeting.

The Shari'a does not intervene in perception or inner states, but it does intervene in inclination, except in one matter among the perceptions of man, which is perceiving the beauty of a woman.

Therefore the Shari'a commanded lowering the gaze, so that a person does not perceive that and then incline toward a conduct to which he has no right, and because perceiving a woman's beauty may push the instincts toward immediate conduct, since instincts do not separate inclination from feeling and perception.

1 - Al-bushra and al-bushara: what is given to the one who is informed of a pleasing news; al-bashr: a verbal noun meaning the good tidings, and each of them is applied to pleasing news. And "bashsharahu" means he informed him of what pleased him. Allah, exalted, says: ﴿He said, "Do you give me good tidings although old age has touched me? Then by what do you give good tidings?" (54)﴾ [al-Hijr]..
2 - Labitha: he remained and settled. "Ma labitha an fa'ala kadhā": he did not hesitate and did not delay, meaning he hastened to do it without any deliberation. His saying, exalted be He, "...fa-ma labitha an ja'a bi-'ijlin hanidh (69)" [Hud] means: he hastened and brought it, and this is an indication of care and hospitality toward the guest [al-Qamus al-Qawim]..
3 - Hanadha al-lahma yahnidhuhu hanadhan: he roasted the meat on stones, so it is haneedh, i.e., roasted. Allah, exalted, says: "...fa-ma labitha an ja'a bi-'ijlin haneedh (69)" [Hud], and its meat is more delicious than boiled or cooked in water. [al-Qamus al-Qawim]..
4 - Istafahu: he chose him, preferred him and favoured him. Allah, exalted, says: "...O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds (42)" [Al 'Imran], i.e., He selected you and favoured you. And Allah, exalted, says: "Allah chooses (yastafi) messengers from among the angels and from among mankind...(75)" [al-Hajj], i.e., He selects the best of them for His messages. [al-Qamus al-Qawim], adapted..
5 - Al-wahy: is applied to the command revealed, as an application of the verbal noun to the object. Allah, exalted, says: "Say: I only warn you by the revelation..(45)" [al-Anbiya'], i.e., by the Qur'an which Allah revealed to me. Al-wahy is also applied to the angel whom Allah sends to the Messenger to convey what Allah has commanded. And His saying, exalted: "It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation..(51)" [al-Shura], i.e., inspiration from Allah, and a casting into the heart of the Messenger swiftly and secretly. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/325]..
6 - "...or from behind a veil...(51)" [al-Shura], i.e., a separation between divinity and humanity, by a way known only to Allah, exalted. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/325]..
7 - "...or that He send a messenger...(51)" [al-Shura], such as Jibril, peace be upon him, who reveals to the Messenger, by Allah's permission, what Allah has commanded. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/325]..
8 - Ista'nasa: his wildness departed; "ista'nasa bihi wa ilayhi": he felt at ease with him. The hamza, sin and ta' indicate seeking, for the most part. So His saying, exalted: "...until you have asked permission and greeted their occupants...(27)" [al-Nur] means: until you seek ease, companionship and contentment, or until you perceive ease and know it. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/37]..
9 - Ma labitha an ja'a: i.e., he hastened to prepare the food and bring it for his guests, and this is strong evidence of the generosity and bounty that characterized Ibrahim, peace be upon him. [al-Qamus al-Qawim], adapted..
10 - Janna al-shay', yajunnuhu janan: he concealed it; the verb includes the meaning of "adhlama," because darkness conceals everything. And janna al-layl: it became dark. [al-Qamus al-Qawim]..
11 - Afala: set, went down beneath the horizon. [Kalimat al-Qur'an]..
12 - Bazighan: rising above the horizon, its light spreading. [Kalimat al-Qur'an]..
13 - Fatara al-shay': split it; and fatara Allah al-khalq: He created them and originated them, so He is Fatir, i.e., He began the creation of the heavens and the earth. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/84]..
14 - Hanifan: turning away from falsehood, standing upright upon the truth. [Lisan al-'Arab]..
15 - Hajjahu: disputed with him over the proof; it is a reciprocal form from both sides, i.e., each presented his argument in order to overcome the other with it. Allah, exalted, says: "And his people disputed with him. He said, 'Do you dispute with me concerning Allah...?' (80)" [al-An'am] [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/143]..
16 - Al-sufsata: sophistry and misleading with the aim of silencing and quieting the opponent. [al-Mu'jam al-Wasit], adapted..
17 - Al-yaqin: firm, clear knowledge free of doubt; it is said, "the best certainty without doubt," and it may refer to death, because there is no doubt about it. Allah, exalted, says: "And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty (99)" [al-Hijr], i.e., death. And Allah, exalted, says: "...So he remained not long, and said, 'I have encompassed that which you have not encompassed, and I have brought to you from Saba' certain news (2)" [al-Naml]. And "ayqana al-amr wa ayqana bihi": he knew it with firm, clear knowledge free of doubt. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/371, 372]..
18 - On the authority of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: "Allah has not sent down any disease except that He has sent down for it a cure." Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (5678) and Ibn Majah in his Sunan (3439)..
19 - Al-qawa'id: plural of qa'ida; the foundation of a building is its base upon which it stands. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/127]..
20 - Wajila yawjalu: he was frightened and feared. Allah, exalted, says: "They said, 'Do not fear...' (53)" [al-Hijr], i.e., do not be frightened nor afraid; and he is wajil, i.e., fearful. And Allah, exalted, says: "...He said, 'Indeed, we are fearful of you' (52)" [al-Hijr]. And Allah, exalted, says: "The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts become fearful..(2)" [al-Anfal]..
21 - Awjasa nafsahu: he concealed fear within himself. Allah, exalted, says of Musa, peace be upon him: "So Musa sensed within himself a fear (67)" [Ta-Ha], and of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: "So he sensed within himself a fear of them..(28)" [al-Dhariyat], i.e., he perceived fright and fear [al-Qamus al-Qawim]..
22 - Al-mawajid: plural of mawjida, which is what the heart perceives and a person finds within himself of feelings of joy, sorrow, contentment, anger and others..
23 - The evidence for this is His saying, mighty and majestic: "Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and guard their private parts. That is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do (30)" [al-Nur]..

Here, the Truth (may He be exalted) mentions the inner perceptions (mawajid) of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) when He says: ﴿And he sensed fear of them. They said: "Do not fear..."﴾ [Hud: 70].

He conveyed the meaning of eagerness (nuzu'i) when He says: ﴿They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace..."﴾ [Hud: 69], which is the time of affirmation and steadying.

The Truth, glory be to Him, said: ﴿...and he did not delay in bringing a roasted calf﴾ [Hud: 69]. A "ḥanīdh" calf is a fat calf roasted on stones, because roasting—as we know—may be done over a flame, over charcoal, or on stones.

Something similar happens in the Arab lands, when they bring a very thin stone, heat it on the fire, and then roast meat on it. This guarantees that no reactions occur between the meat and the stone, whereas reactions do occur with iron or charcoal; therefore this is the cleanest method of roasting.

Or the phrase ﴿...a roasted calf﴾ [Hud: 69] means: the fat drips from it after roasting.

And the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him: ﴿...so he did not delay in bringing a roasted calf﴾ [Hud: 69], is because the nature of our master Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is love of guests and honouring them.

It is the custom of the noble to hasten in honouring the guest and serving him food, and the generous person is the one who does this, because he does not know how long the guest has gone without food. If the guest is hungry, he eats; and if he is full, he declares it.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says what happened after Ibrahim (peace be upon him) brought them the roasted calf: ﴿But when he saw that their hands did not reach towards it, he viewed them with suspicion (nakarahum)[2] and sensed fear of them (awjasa)[3]. They said, "Do not fear; indeed we have been sent to the people of Lot."﴾ [Hud: 70].

When Ibrahim saw that their hands did not reach the food, he suspected evil and "nakarahum"—that is, he found them strange and disapproved that they had not eaten from the food he had offered them. Did Ibrahim know that they were angels?

Ibrahim (peace be upon him) knew that they were angels from their speech.

This is explained by the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him, in another place in the Qur'an: ﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace," he said, "Indeed we are fearful of you." They said, "Do not fear; we give you good tidings of a knowing boy." He said, "Do you give me good tidings although old age has touched me? Then what is it you give tidings of?" They said, "We have given you good tidings of truth, so do not be of the despairing." He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?" He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?" They said, "We have been sent to a criminal people"﴾ [al-Hijr: 52–58].

Therefore, they did not say to him what they said to Lot (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed, we are messengers of your Lord﴾ [Hud: 81].

Here, when they said to Ibrahim (peace be upon him): ﴿...Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 70], this means that they understood that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) knew they were angels, because an angel may take the form of a human, just as Gabriel (peace be upon him) appeared in human form before our master Muhammad (ﷺ).

Likewise, the jinn have the ability to take forms, but there is a difference between the form-taking of an angel and that of a jinn. The jinn, when they take a form, are governed by that form: if one takes the form of a man, you can seize him and harm him.

Did not the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say:

"Indeed an 'ifrit of the jinn escaped from me last night to cut off my prayer, but God enabled me over him, so I seized him, and I wanted to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque so that you could all look at him. Then I remembered the supplication of my brother Solomon:

﴿He said, "My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not belong to anyone after me; indeed You are the Bestower."﴾ [Sad: 35]

So I sent him back, humbled."[7] So, when the jinn take a form, they are governed by that form, and we may strike them as an example; but when an angel takes a form, the form does not govern him.

The governance of the form over the jinn is what protects us from our fears. He also fears us just as we fear him; therefore the jinn appear in a form only for a brief moment, then vanish immediately, because he fears that you may have learned that the form he took governs him and that you can destroy him. Thus the jinn fear mankind.

The Truth, glory be to Him, willed this matter so that the jinn would not frighten people.

Here the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿But when he saw that their hands did not reach towards it, he viewed them with suspicion (nakarahum)...﴾ [Hud: 70].

The word ﴿nakarahum﴾ requires us to consider the root n-k-r. Both "nakar" and "ankar" are used in the Qur'an.[8]

The poet says: "You disowned me, though what you disowned of the events was only the white hair and the bald head."
Linguistic usage shows that reprehensible forms of conduct are called "munkarāt" (things disapproved), that is, a person disapproves of them by his natural disposition.

Here, when Ibrahim (peace be upon him) saw that their hands did not reach the roasted calf, he "nakarahum" and sensed fear within himself; they noticed this and said: ﴿...Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lot﴾ [Hud: 70]. This was a recognition of those who had come, and he became reassured that his people had not done anything deserving punishment. Especially since the history books say that Ibrahim's wife said to him: "Will you not take your nephew into your care here?" because his people were about to be overtaken by God's punishment.

When she heard that the messengers had been sent only to the people of Lot, she understood from her insight[11] and smiled, because she had become alert to this matter.

In another verse the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿They said, "Indeed we have been sent to a criminal people, to send upon them stones of clay, marked[12] by your Lord for the transgressors."﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 32–34].

---

1 - "An" here means "until" (ḥattā), as said by the great grammarians, related by Qadi Ibn al-'Arabi. The meaning is: he did not delay in bringing a calf. Mentioned by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (4/3382).

2 - The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urged the honouring of guests. On the authority of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest; whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him maintain the ties of kinship; and whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent." Agreed upon. Recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (6018) and likewise Muslim in his Sahih (47).

3 - "Nakara": he felt strange toward him, shunned him, and did not feel at ease with him. [al-Qamus al-Qawim]. You say: "nakartuka," "ankartuka," and "istankartuka" when you find him other than what you knew. See al-Qurtubi (4/3384).

4 - "Wajasa" and "awjasa": to feel fear. "Awjasa fi nafsihi": he concealed fear within himself. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he sensed fear of them﴾ [Hud: 70] means he perceived alarm and fear. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So Moses sensed fear within himself﴾ [Ta-Ha: 67], meaning he concealed fear within himself when he saw the sorcerers' acts. [al-Qamus al-Qawim].

5 - "Al-qanitun": those whose hope of good has been cut off or who have despaired of it. "Al-qunut" is an intensive form: extremely despairing, devoid of security. [al-Qamus al-Qawim].

6 - "Tafallata": it confronted me suddenly, unexpectedly.

7 - Recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (3423) and Muslim in his Sahih (541), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).

8 - The word "nakar" occurs in His saying: ﴿But when he saw that their hands did not reach towards it, he viewed them with suspicion (nakarahum)...﴾ [Hud: 70]. And He said of Solomon: ﴿He said, "Disguise her throne for her..."﴾ [al-Naml: 41]. As for "ankara," He said: ﴿And He shows you His signs, so which of the signs of Allah do you deny?﴾ [Ghafir: 81], and He said: ﴿And among the factions are those who deny part of it...﴾ [al-Ra'd: 36], and His saying: ﴿They recognize the favour of Allah, then they deny it, and most of them are disbelievers.﴾ [al-Nahl: 83].

9 - The poet combined the two forms. It is said: "nakarta" for what you see with your eyes, and "ankarta" for what you perceive with your heart. Said by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (4/3384).

10 - "Al-kanf" and "al-kanfa": the side of a thing. "Kanafa al-rajula al-rajul": he took him under his protection, in his care and support. "Kanaftu al-rajul": I shielded and protected the man. [See Lisan al-'Arab].

11 - "Al-firasa": insight in looking, careful consideration and reflection upon a thing, and perceiving it. "Tafarrusa": to discern something in a person so that it turns out as you discerned it; this occurs in one of two ways: 1. What God places in the hearts of His friends by way of unveilings; 2. What one learns through evidence and experience, by which one knows people's conditions. [See Lisan al-'Arab], with additions from us.

12 - "Musawwama 'inda rabbika": that is, bearing marks with the names of those to be punished. "Sawwama 'ala al-qawm": he raided them and wrought destruction and ruin among them. God said: ﴿...your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels marked [musawwimin]﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 125], meaning marking themselves and their horses with signs, or raiding the disbelievers. And His saying: ﴿and the branded horses...﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 14], meaning sent out to pasture, or marked with signs. And His saying: ﴿Their mark is on their faces...﴾ [al-Fath: 29], meaning the signs of their faith are light upon their faces. [al-Qamus al-Qawim].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 11, verse 71:

Then the Truthful (al-Haqq), glory be to Him, says:

﴿And his wife was standing, so she laughed, and We gave her good tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob.﴾ (71)

When his wife was standing to serve the guests, and heard the words of the angels, she was reassured that there would be no punishment upon their people, and her insight was confirmed, so she laughed, and God increased her joy. The angels gave her the good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob.

After the averting of the punishment and the explanation of the punishment for another people who are criminals, comes the good news of the fulfilment of what Abraham, peace be upon him, and his wife had been yearning for, even though its time had already passed, for Abraham's wife had reached the age of ninety, and he had reached the age of one hundred and twenty years.[4] In this there is a favour upon Abraham through the coming of a son's son as well. Likewise God, glory be to Him, bestows favour upon His servants when He says: ﴿And God made for you spouses from among yourselves, and made for you from your spouses sons and grandchildren (ḥafadah)...﴾ (72) [al-Nahl].

1 - She is Sarah, the wife of Abraham, peace be upon him, from his people. She is the mother of Isaac, peace be upon him. The child came to her when she was of advanced age, after Hagar had borne Ishmael, peace be upon him, to Abraham.

2 - On the authority of Sahl ibn Sa'd that Abu Usayd al-Sa'idi came to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and invited him to his wedding feast, and his wife was their servant that day, and she was the bride. He said: "Do you know what she gave the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace? She soaked some dates in a tor (bowl) from the night before." Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (5176), Ahmad in his Musnad (3/498), and Ibn Majah in his Sunan (1912).

3 - Sabā, yasbū, sabwan: to incline and to love. God the Exalted said: ﴿...And if You do not turn away from me their plot, I would incline towards them and be among the ignorant﴾ [Yusuf] (33). Asbū: I incline; and sabā ilā al-shay': he yearned for and longed for it. [al-Qamus al-Qawim].

4 - Mujahid said: Sarah was ninety-nine years old. Ibn Ishaq said: she was ninety. Other views were also given. As for Abraham, it is said he was one hundred and twenty years old, and it is said he was one hundred years old. Related by al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (4/3388).

5 - Ḥafadah: the children's children (grandchildren). Al-ḥafid: the helper and servant, and the son of a son; its plural is ḥafad and ḥafd. Ḥafada and ḥafd in his work: he was light and quick and hastened in it, so he is ḥafid, and he is ḥafīd. The helper, servant, or son's son is called ḥafid because of his alacrity and lightness in assistance and service. [al-Qamus al-Qawim, 1/161].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 11, verse 72:

﴿And Allah has made for you from yourselves spouses, and has made for you from your spouses sons and grandsons(1)...﴾ [An-Nahl: 72].

Therefore the Truthful, glorified is He, said:

﴿...So We gave her the glad tidings of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ [Hud: 71]: a man must have a son, and he loves even more to see his son's son, because this represents an extension of himself.

Thus the glad tidings followed one another. The angels declared that they had come to punish the people of Lot, those with whom Abraham, peace be upon him, had disagreed because of the abominations they had brought, and also because Abraham, peace be upon him, and his wife knew that they had not committed any act that angers Allah, the Exalted.

The third of the glad tidings was the boy. This had been a long-held dream of Abraham's wife, peace be upon him, because she was barren. Abraham's wife received the first glad tidings with laughter, and received the glad tidings of a son with astonishment(2).

On this, the Truthful, glorified is He, said:

﴿She said, "Oh woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this my husband(3) is an old man? Indeed, this is an amazing thing!" ﴾ [Hud: 72]

The amazing thing is that which contravenes the customary laws of the universe. But there is a difference between the laws (4) and the Creator of the laws, who is able to break the laws.

Here is our master Abraham saying in another place: ﴿Do you give me glad tidings although old age has touched me...?﴾ [Al-Hijr: 54]. He did not use here the words of Abraham's wife, who said: ﴿Oh woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this my husband is an old man...?﴾ [Hud: 72]. The naming of the husband as "ba'l" contains great precision, because the ba'l is the one who manages the affairs of the one he owns (mab'ul) and does not make him need anyone.

Likewise, the husband manages the affairs of his wife in matters that her father and her brother cannot manage, namely the sense of femininity and fertility, which is the most important thing a woman seeks.

Also, the palm tree is called ba'l, because it does not ask its cultivator to water it; the palm is content with what it draws from the earth and the rain that falls on it from the sky(5).

For this reason a type of fava bean is called "the ba'li fava bean," which is the one that does not need irrigation.

So: the ba'l is the husband who takes charge of his wife's affairs, so that he does not make her need anyone else in anything at all.

1 - Hafadah (ḥafadah): grandchildren. Al-ḥafid means helper and servant, and the son of a son; its plural is ḥafad and ḥafadah. Ḥafada in his work means he was light and quick and hastened in it, so he is ḥafid, and he is ḥafid(a). He called the helper, servant, or son's son ḥafid for his activity and lightness in helping and serving [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/161].
2 - The Lord of Might, glorified is He, says about this in Surat adh-Dhariyat: ﴿...And they gave him glad tidings of a learned boy. Then his wife came forward in a loud cry, and struck her face, and said, "An old barren woman!" They said, "Thus has your Lord said. Indeed, He is the Wise, the All-Knowing."﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 28-30]. Ṣakk al-wajh: striking the face in amazement, and it is a metaphor for astonishment [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/380].
3 - Ba'l: the husband and the wife. It is a verbal noun named by its own form, so it is not feminized. Its plural is bu'ulah. Allah says: ﴿And this my husband, an old man...﴾ [Hud: 72]. And Allah says: ﴿And their husbands have more right to take them back...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], meaning their husbands have more right to take them back after a revocable divorce, and after an irrevocable single divorce or two irrevocable divorces, by a new contract [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/76].
The husband of a woman is called ba'l because he is her lord and owner. Mubā'alah means intercourse. Al-bi'āl means marriage. Tabā'alat al-mar'ah means the woman obeyed her husband; tabā'alat lahu means she adorned herself for him. A woman of good tab'ul is one who is obedient to her husband and loving toward him [Lisan al-Arab].
4 - Al-nawamis: the divine laws to which the universe is subject.
5 - Ibn Manzur mentioned it in Lisan al-Arab [root: b-'-l]: istab'ala al-mawdi' and al-nakhl: it became ba'l, with roots firmly set in water, independent of irrigation and of channeling water to it through a river or a ditch. [Al-'Athur: it is the well].

Here is the wife of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) wondering at the matter of childbearing, because this is a strange thing that happens unexpectedly; for this reason the angels respond to her.

The Truthful, glory be to Him, says about that:

﴿They said: "Do you wonder at the command of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy, Glorious."﴾

Wonder, then, arises only from a human law, whereas the Supreme Power, glory be to Him, has absolute freedom of power to break the law (nāmūs). And miracles came from breaking these laws, to establish the truth of the message from Allah, Exalted. Miracles are thus something that breaks the customary order of the cosmos.

The story that happened to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and his wife was repeated in the story of Zakariyya (peace be upon him). Allah, the Truthful, gave Maryam (peace be upon her) the glad tidings that reminded Zakariyya (peace be upon him) when he asked her: ﴿Where did this come to you from?...﴾ [Āl ʿImrān], and Maryam said:

﴿"It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account."﴾ [Āl ʿImrān].

So, the reckoning happens between creatures and one another, not between the Creator, glory be to Him, and His creation.

For this reason the words of the Truthful, Exalted, come: ﴿There Zakariyya prayed to his Lord...﴾ [Āl ʿImrān].

Since Zakariyya (peace be upon him) was reminded by the words of Maryam: ﴿"...Indeed Allah provides for whom He wills without account."﴾ [Āl ʿImrān],

it was his right to pray: ﴿He said: "My Lord, grant me from Yourself offspring..."﴾ [Āl ʿImrān]. So Allah, glory be to Him and Exalted, revealed to him: ﴿"O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good tidings of a boy whose name is Yahya; We have not assigned to anyone before him that name."﴾ [Maryam]. That is: the Truthful, glory be to Him, did not merely grant him a son, but also named him with a name that no one had been given before.

The naming of Allah, Exalted, differs from the naming of humans. If some people later named some of their sons "Yahya," they did so out of good omen (fāl) (1), hoping the son would live.

But when the Truthful, glory be to Him, names something, He named him "Yahya" so that he would indeed live, reach the age of maturity, and then death would not come to him; therefore Yahya was killed and became a martyr, and the martyr is alive with his Lord, death never coming to him (2).

This is the opposite of human naming, since a person may name his son "Sa'id" (happy) and the son lives his life in the utmost misery.

The poet says about the person who named his son "Yahya": "I named him Yahya so that he would live, but there was no way to avert the decree of Allah concerning him."

When we return to the fact that Maryam (peace be upon her) was the one who drew attention to the matter of provision from Allah, we find that Zakariyya (peace be upon him) prayed, and mentioned that he was advanced in age and that his wife was barren.

Zakariyya (peace be upon him) must have known that the Truthful, glory be to Him, knows everything from eternity (3), and so Allah, glory be to Him, willed to reassure Zakariyya (peace be upon him) that He would give him a son and name him. The words of the Truthful, Exalted, come: ﴿"Thus says your Lord..."﴾ [Maryam]. Since the Truthful, glory be to Him, is the One who decreed, there is no repeller of what He wills; therefore He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿"...It is easy for Me, and I created you before, when you were nothing."﴾ [Maryam].

Thus the events followed after Maryam reminded Zakariyya (peace be upon him) of the matter of breaking the laws, to which she herself was subjected afterward, when the angel appeared to her in the form of a man and gave her the good news of a boy named the Messiah, Jesus son of Maryam (peace be upon him). Maryam wondered how this would happen, though no man had touched her, and the angel reminded her that it was she on whose tongue Allah, the Truthful, had caused His words to be spoken during her conversation with Zakariyya (peace be upon him): ﴿"...Indeed Allah provides for whom He wills without account."﴾ [Āl ʿImrān].

Reassurance was necessary for her, because her bearing the Messiah Jesus (peace be upon him) without a father was a matter of public appearance, which must be received while she was trustworthy, not doubted or accused.

The verse we are discussing here concerns the wife of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) when the glad tidings of the child came to her, and how the angels made clear to her that there is nothing strange in what Allah has decreed and willed, contrary to the prevailing law in His creation; for the mercy of Allah, blessed and exalted, encompassing every good, has embraced the People of the Prophetic House, and among that mercy and those blessings is the granting of children at other than the usual time (4).

For this reason the Truthful, glory be to Him, said here: ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house...﴾ [Hūd].

The Truthful, glory be to Him, concludes the verse with His words, Exalted: ﴿"...Indeed, He is Praiseworthy, Glorious."﴾ [Hūd]. That is: He, glory be to Him, deserves praise in His essence, and everything that proceeds from Him requires praise from His servants; there is no limit to His goodness and beneficence, and Allah, Exalted, possesses the absolute attributes of glory.

The word "Ḥamīd" (praiseworthy), linguistically, is of the pattern fa'īl, and it occurs with two meanings: either in the sense of the active participle, as in our saying "Allah is Raḥīm" meaning that He shows mercy to His creation; or in the sense of the passive participle, as in our saying "qatīl" meaning "maqtūl" (killed).

The word "Ḥamīd" here comes with both meanings together: "ḥāmid" (one who praises) and "maḥmūd" (one who is praised), like the words of the Truthful, Exalted, about Himself as "al-Shakūr" (the Appreciative); for He, glory be to Him, thanks whoever thanks Him for His blessings by obeying Him, and Allah, glory be to Him, is "Ḥamīd" because He praises whoever obeys Him with obedience springing from faith, and Allah, glory be to Him, is "Maḥmūd" by those upon whom He has bestowed His abundant blessings.

Allah, glory be to Him, is al-Majīd (the Glorious), who gives before being asked.

For this reason we find a knower of Allah, Exalted, to whom a beggar came; he brought out a purse and placed it in his hand, then returned to his family weeping. His wife said to him: "What makes you weep, when you have given him his due by his asking?" He said: "I weep because I left him to ask, and I should not have allowed him to stand in the position of a beggar."

The Truthful, glory be to Him and Exalted, gave us before we even knew how to ask, such as His giving to the fetus in its mother's womb, which has not learned speech or asking.

And the Truthful, glory be to Him and Exalted, in every scene of the Qur'an gives a social lesson drawn from the religion. Here is our master Ibrahim (peace be upon him) offering the roasted calf to the guests, to teach us that if a guest comes to you and you offer him food and he does not eat, you should not remove the food from in front of him, but must ask him to eat. If he refuses firmly and says, "I have eaten before I came to you," then you may remove the food from in front of him after you have insisted on him eating.

Some knowers (5) relate that when our master Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said, "Will you not eat?", the angels said: "We do not eat unless we are paid the price of the food." Ibrahim said, by what Allah had given him of the wisdom of prophethood and inspired insight: "Its price is that you mention the name of Allah at its beginning and praise Him at its end" (6).

If you approach a meal and say at its beginning, "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," and when you finish it you say, "Praise be to Allah," you have fulfilled the right of the food, in confirmation of the words of the Truthful, Exalted: ﴿"Then you will be asked that Day about the pleasure."﴾ [al-Takāthur].

Thus the Truthful, glory be to Him, has shown us that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and his wife were reassured that the angels had come to them with good tidings, and that they did not intend any harm to Ibrahim or his people, but were charged with punishing the people of Lūṭ.

Here the Truthful, glory be to Him, says:

﴿So when fear had left Ibrahim and the good tidings had come to him, he began to plead with Us concerning the people of Lūṭ.﴾

1 - Anā: an interrogative particle meaning "from where." It also comes meaning "how," as in His words: ﴿"So come to your tilth however you wish..."﴾ [al-Baqarah], i.e., how you wish, on condition of following the upright nature indicated by the verse. In some verses it is suitable for both meanings, as in His words: ﴿"How can there be for me a boy..."﴾ [Āl ʿImrān]. [al-Qāmūs al-Qawīm p. 41, n. 1].
2 - Al-Fāl: the opposite of ṭiyara (ill omen); its plural is fu'ūl and afūl; from it comes tafā'ul (optimism), which is expecting good. [Mukhtār al-Qāmūs], adapted.
3 - Ibn Kathīr said in Qiṣaṣ al-Anbiyā' [p. 390]: "They mentioned for his killing several causes, the most famous being that some kings of that time in Damascus wanted to marry one of his close relatives, or someone whom it was not lawful for him to marry; Yahya (peace be upon him) forbade him from that, so she held a grudge against him. When she had what she wanted from the king, she asked him for the blood of Yahya, and he granted it to her; she sent someone who killed him and brought his head and blood on a platter to her. It is said that she died immediately on the spot."
4 - On this the Truthful, glory be to Him, says: ﴿"And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, provided for."﴾ [Āl ʿImrān].
5 - Zakariyya said: ﴿"...My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened and my head has shone with white hair, and I have never been, in calling upon You, my Lord, unblessed."﴾ [Maryam]. And after his being given good news of Yahya he said: ﴿"My Lord, how can there be for me a boy when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?"﴾ [Maryam]. Mujāhid said: "ʿitiyyan" means the bones have become withered. Ibn Kathīr said in his tafsīr [3/112]: "No potency or intercourse remained in him."
6 - Al-Azal: eternity; its origin is "lam yazal" (he has not ceased). Abū Manṣūr said: from it is their saying, "this is an azalī thing," i.e., eternal [Lisān al-ʿArab].
7 - Al-Qurṭubī said in his tafsīr [4/3389]: "Among those gifts and blessings is that all the prophets and messengers were among the descendants of Ibrahim and Sarah." Adapted.
8 - He is ʿUmar ibn Dīnār al-Jumaḥī, by clientage, Abū Muḥammad al-Athram; he was the mufti of the people of Makkah, of Persian origin, born in Ṣanʿāʾ in 46 AH and died in Makkah [126 AH] at the age of 81. Shuʿba said: "I have not seen anyone more reliable in ḥadīth than him." [al-Aʿlām of al-Zirikli 5/77].
9 - This report is mentioned by al-Suyūṭī in al-Durr al-Manthūr [4/450], and at its end that the angels looked at one another and said: "For this Allah took him as a close friend (khalīl)," and he attributed it to Ibn al-Mundhir from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār.
10 - Ra'ahu al-shay' yarū'uhu, ruʿban: it struck his ruʿ, i.e., his heart; al-ruʿ (with a damma on the rāʾ) means the heart. And His words, Exalted: ﴿"So when the fear had left Ibrahim..."﴾ [Hūd] mean: fear and alarm left him. [al-Qāmūs al-Qawīm].
11 - Al-Jadal: dispute over opinion and intensity of contention. He, Exalted, said: ﴿"...And man is most of anything contentious."﴾ [al-Kahf], i.e., most exaggerated in contention and in supporting falsehood without right. [al-Qāmūs al-Qawīm].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 11, verse 74:

Al-jidal (debate, argumentation) is that you take an argument from your opponent and give him an argument in return, in order to reach the truth. Al-jidal differs from al-mira' (contentious disputation). Al-mira' means that you know the truth but argue with falsehood, because you do not want to reach the truth.

Allah, glorified is He, has forbidden us from al-mira', and has commanded us to argue on the condition that the argument be conducted in the best manner.

Here Allah, glorified is He, shows us that Ibrahim, after fear had left him and the good tidings had come to him that Allah, exalted is He, would grant him a boy, and Ibrahim had learned from the angels that they were going to punish the people of Lut:

﴿They said: Indeed, we have been sent to a criminal people. (32) To send down upon them stones of clay (33) marked from your Lord.. (34)﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat]. Ibrahim's arguing about the punishment of the people of Lut was not a rejection of Allah's command, but a request for respite, so that perhaps they would believe, for the heart of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was a merciful heart.

For this reason, Allah, exalted is He, gives the cause of the argument in His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was forbearing, grieving (over them), turning back (to Allah). (75)﴾:

1. Mara'ahu yumaruhu mumarata wa mira': he debated with him and argued with him. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿...So do not argue concerning them except in an apparent manner, and do not inquire about them among them from anyone. (22)﴾ [Al-Kahf], meaning: do not argue with the People of the Book concerning the matter of the People of the Cave except with clear and easy argument. And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you dispute? (55)﴾ [An-Najm], meaning: would you doubt. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim].
2. Musawwamah: meaning, upon it are seals bearing the names of those to be punished. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the marked horses...(14)﴾ [Al 'Imran], meaning: marked with signs, or sent out to pasture. And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Their mark is on their faces...(29)﴾ [Al-Fath], meaning: the sign of their faith is light upon their faces. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim].
3. Awwah: an intensive form, meaning one who sighs much, and it came to mean supplication to Allah in worship and regret over sins. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim].
4. Anaba al-'abd ila rabbihi: he returned to Him, repented, and abandoned sins. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿...Upon Him I have relied, and to Him I turn back. (88)﴾ [Hud], meaning: to Him I repent and return. Munib is an active participle. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a heart turning back (to Him). (33)﴾ [Qaf], meaning: with a heart returning to Allah. The plural of munib came in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Turning back to Him and fear Him...(31)﴾ [Ar-Rum], meaning: returning, repentant to Him; that is, be repentant and be God-fearing. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 11, verse 75:

Idha (thus, then): the reason for his arguing is that he was forbearing (halim), not hastening to punishment, and awwah, that is, one who sighs (yata'awwahu) from the heart. Ta'awwuh is tenderness of heart. If the sighing is directed upward, it means fear that one has not fulfilled the right of Allah the Exalted; if the sighing is for those below, it is mercy and compassion.

Therefore Ibrahim (peace be upon him) asked Allah the Exalted to postpone the punishment for the people of Lut, perhaps they would believe. His sighing here was directed to Allah the Exalted, and toward these ignorant people regarding the painful punishment awaiting them.

The Truthful, Glorified One described Ibrahim's attributes as "munib," that is, one who returns to the judgment and to the truth in his affairs.

Did not the Truthful, Glorified One say in another place in His Noble Book: ﴿And the prayer of forgiveness of Ibrahim for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him...﴾ (9:114).

After Ibrahim (peace be upon him) sought the truth and turned in repentance to it, Allah the Exalted and Most High shows us the manifestation of repentance in His saying: ﴿But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him...﴾ (9:114). Here, in the verse we are contemplating, which clarified Ibrahim's sighing before Allah the Mighty and Majestic and his sighing out of mercy for those who did not believe, namely the people of Lut, Ibrahim's argument also included what the Truthful, Glorified One said in Surat al-Ankabut: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Ibrahim with good tidings, they said, "Indeed, we will destroy the people of this town. Indeed, its people have been wrongdoers." (31) He said, "Indeed, Lut is there..."﴾ (32) (29:31-32).

Ibrahim's question to the angels was: how will you destroy the people of this town when among them is one who believes in Allah, and at their head a prophet of Allah, Lut (peace be upon him)? The angels replied: ﴿...We are most knowing of who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife; she was of those who remained behind﴾ (29:32).

It is as if Ibrahim, Khalil al-Rahman, knew that the presence of believers among disbelievers in one town permits him to argue on behalf of all the people of the town.

Ibrahim receives the response here in Surat Hud in the following verse:

﴿O Ibrahim, leave this. Indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and indeed, there will reach them a punishment that cannot be turned back.﴾ (11:76)

1 - "Wa'ada shay'an yaiduhu wa'dan wa 'idatan": he informed him that he would fulfill it for him, or would give it to him. It is a verb that takes two objects, and one of the two objects may be omitted when it is known. "Al-Maw'idah" is a mimi verbal noun and also a noun of time or place. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿except for a promise he had made to him...﴾ (9:114), meaning: a single promise made one time [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/343].

2 - "Min al-Ghabirin": that is, among those who remained behind in the town for destruction, or the meaning is that she was among those who had passed on, that is, among those who perished. It is said: "mada" and "dhahaba" mean the same as "halaka" and "mata" (died) [al-Qamus al-Qawim].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 11, verse 76:

The saying of the angels: ﴿O Abraham, turn away from this...﴾ (76) [Hud]: meaning, they informed Abraham that the matter of punishing those among the people of Lot who did not believe is a decree that has been finalized and settled. They had come to carry it out, not merely to threaten. And they informed Abraham: ﴿Indeed, there has come the command of your Lord...﴾ (76) [Hud]. Since the command has come from Allah, Abraham, peace be upon him, being one who turns back to Allah (munib), knows that any command of Allah the Exalted must be carried out, so he must accept the command of the Truth, glorified is He: ﴿...and indeed, there will come to them a punishment that cannot be averted﴾ (76) [Hud]. That is: no one is able to avert the punishment of Allah. Just as there is a promise from Allah the Exalted that is not false(1), so there is also a punishment that cannot be averted(2).

It is related(3) that Abraham, peace be upon him, in his argument said to the angels: "If there are fifty in the people of Lot who have believed in Allah the Exalted, will you punish them?" They said: "No." He said: "And if there are ten among them who believe in Allah, will you punish them?" They said: "No." He said: "And if there is one among them, who is Lot?" The angels responded: ﴿We know best who is in it. We will surely save him and his family, except his wife...﴾ (32) [al-Ankabut]. The argument ended, and the angels went on to their task, which was to bring down the punishment upon the people of Lot.

The Exalted says: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed for them and felt constrained in his position, and said, "This is a trying day."﴾ (44): that is, Lot felt distress and was constrained in his position. The word "dhar'" (constraint, lit. "reach of the arm") is derived from "dhira'" (the forearm), which contains the palm and fingers, and with which we push things away, and with which one reaches toward something. If your arm cannot reach it, you say: "I was constrained by it (ḍiqtu bihi dhar'an)," meaning my hand could not reach it, and it is a matter beyond my strength and capacity, and beyond what Allah has given me of tools and means.

And what was it that distressed Lot about the arrival of the angels?

It is said: because the angels had come in the known form of beauty. When it is said, "So-and-so is an angel" (malak), it means that his form is beautiful(6).

Lot, peace be upon him, knew that the affliction of his people was the practice of approaching males, and his wife knew of this affliction, but her position regarding it was not Lot's position; she welcomed that affliction.

It is said that she became aware of the arrival of handsome men, without knowing that they were angels of punishment, and she went up to the roof of the house and clapped, so that the people might notice her. No one paid attention to her, so she lit a fire, and the people took notice of her, and she gestured to them with what signifies the arrival of guests distinguished by beauty(7).

Here Lot, peace be upon him, said: ﴿...This is a trying day﴾ (77) [Hud].

1 - This was said concerning the people of Thamud with their prophet Salih, for Allah threatened them that they would remain and enjoy their homes for three days, after which the punishment of Allah would come upon them because of their hamstringing of the she-camel. He, glorified is He, says: ﴿But they hamstrung her, so he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied."﴾ (65) [Hud]..
2 - "Not to be averted": that is, not turned away from them nor repelled. [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/3392]..
3 - Al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur [4/460] and attributed it to ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim, from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman..
4 - One says: "Dāqa bi-l-amr dharʿan" and "dharāʿan": that is, he could not bear it, nor had the strength to endure it, and it weighed heavily upon him because of the constraint. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿...and he was constrained for them (77)﴾ [Hud], that is, the constraint pressed heavily upon him because of their presence, out of fear for them from his people. [al-Qamus al-Qawim]. And "wa-ḍāqa bihim dharʿan": his capacity was weakened in arranging their deliverance. [Kalimat al-Qur'an by Shaykh Husnayn Makhluf]..
5 - "Yawm ʿaṣīb": its evil and trial are severe. [Kalimat al-Qur'an]..
6 - This is what the women of Joseph, peace be upon him, said when the wife of the Aziz brought him in to them: ﴿...So when they saw him, they greatly admired him and cut their hands and said, "Allah forbid! This is not a human. This is none but a noble angel."﴾ (31) [Yusuf]..
7 - And that was her betrayal of her husband Lot, peace be upon him: she would point out Lot's guests to her people so that they might commit the abomination with them. The Lord of Glory said concerning the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot: ﴿They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them...﴾ (10) [al-Tahrim].

Meaning: a day of severe distress.

It is said: "a yawm 'aṣīb" (a grievous day) and "a yawm 'aṣbaṣ" (a harsh day) (1). From the same root is "al-'uṣba" (2), meaning a group of people who support one another in a matter, so that the individual is strengthened by their collective strength. And indeed, Lot's suspicion was confirmed.

On this, the Truth, glorified is He, says regarding that:

﴿And his people came rushing toward him, and before that they had been doing evil deeds. He said: "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you a man of sound judgment?" (78)﴾

1 - Al-Farra' said: "yawm 'aṣīb" and "'aṣbaṣ" mean severe. It was also said that it means extremely hot. Abu al-'Ala' said: "yawm 'aṣbaṣ" is a cold day with abundant clouds, in which nothing of the sky is visible. [Lisan al-'Arab, root ʿ-ṣ-b]
2 - Al-'uṣba and al-'iṣāba: a group of between ten and forty people. The Exalted said: ﴿And we are a group (ʿuṣba)...(14)﴾ [Yusuf]. Al-Akhfash said: al-'uṣba and al-'iṣāba are a group that has no singular form. [Lisan al-'Arab, root ʿ-ṣ-b]
3 - Al-hara': walking in agitation and haste; one comes "yuhra'" (rushing), and "uhrii'a" (passive) so he is "muhra'" (driven), trembling from weakness or fear. Al-mahrū' is one afflicted with madness who falls down. [Mukhtar al-Qamus]
4 - Al-rashīd: one of the Beautiful Names of Allah, though Allah is not described by it in the Qur'an. Rashada, yarshudu, rushdan and rushadan: he attained the right way, goodness and truth. Al-rushd is the opposite of error and misguidance, and the opposite of foolishness and poor management. "Balagha rushdahu" means he reached full maturity of intellect and good management of affairs. The Exalted said: ﴿Right guidance has become distinct from error...(256)﴾ [al-Baqara]. He also said: ﴿And We had certainly given Abraham his sound judgment...(51)﴾ [al-Anbiya'], i.e., We guided him to truth, goodness and rightness. And He said, quoting the disbelievers: ﴿...Indeed, you are the forbearing, the sound of judgment (87)﴾ [Hud], and their intent was to mock the Prophet of Allah Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) by describing him as the only forbearing and sound-judged one among them, while they believed the opposite. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/266, adapted]

**Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 11, verse 78:**

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And his people came hastening towards him...﴾ (78):

That is, they hurried towards him in a crowd. A person who has not become accustomed to evil and has no practice in it is hesitant and fearful, whereas one who has practice in it approaches evil boldly and eagerly.

The word "yuhra'una" (يهرعون, "hastening") is one of the wondrous words of the Arabic language. In the words of the language you find a verb that has a subject, as when we say "yadribu Zaydun 'Amran" (يضرب زيد عمرا), meaning that the striker is "Zayd" and the one struck is "'Amr." And we say "yudrabu 'Amrun" (يضرب عمرو), meaning that we have made the verb passive, and "'Amr" is called the "na'ib al-fa'il" (deputy of the subject, i.e. the grammatical object standing in for the subject in the passive).

As for the verb "yuhra'" (يهرع), we never find anyone saying "yuhra'" (يُهرع) without a subject (fa'il) following it, not a deputy of the subject (na'ib al-fa'il). It is like the verb "junna" (جن, "to be possessed/driven mad"): is there anyone who brings madness upon himself, or is it madness that comes to him? No one knows the cause of madness; therefore the word is put in the passive, but what follows it is a subject. This is one of the miracles of Qur'anic eloquence.

Likewise we say "zukima fulan" (زُكم فلان, "so-and-so caught a cold"): who afflicted him with the cold? We do not know any apparent cause of the cold.

So, when the doer is unknown, we put the verb in the passive, but what follows it is a subject.

As for the Almighty's saying: ﴿hastening towards him...﴾ (78), it shows that they came in a rush, as if they were in love with what they were going towards, because each of them had practice in that shameful deed; or that each of them was going to what he loves without hesitation, rushing of his own accord and being pushed by others, just as you say: "We will distribute supplies free of charge" — here you see people pushing one another, each of them on his own initiative, while another pushes him back.

The people of Lot were accustomed to that vice.

The Almighty says of them: ﴿And before that they used to commit evil deeds...﴾ (78): that is, this matter was beloved among them, they were practised in it, it was light upon their hearts, and no shame restrained them from it.

Shame means that some people commit an evil deed and others fear to do it, but if they all love that evil, no one will be ashamed before another (1).

And what was the position of Lot, peace be upon him, on this grievous day? They came upon him quickly, in a throng and in a rush, while he knew their intentions and knew their past. Lot, peace be upon him, thought of diverting them away by means of something of the same kind as their rush.

The Almighty says: ﴿He said: "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you..."﴾ (78). He said this because woman was created for that purpose, and it was possible for them to marry his daughters.

In the days of Lot, peace be upon him, custom did not prevent a believer from marrying his daughter to a non-believer; and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married one of his daughters to 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab and another to Abu al-'As ibn al-Rabi', before the Almighty forbade the marriage of a believing woman to a non-believer.

Was the intended meaning: his daughters from his own loins, or the daughters of his people, or the daughters of those who believed in him? It has been said that none believed in Allah except Lot and his two daughters, so how could a marriage to two daughters be [offered] to all this number of men pressing forward?

It has been said that he sought out the noble, powerful men who held the decision in their hands, and wished to appease them with this marriage, so that perhaps they would turn back from indecencies and evil deeds; and in this would be purity for them, and thereby they would preserve his dignity before his guests.

Lot, peace be upon him, says: ﴿So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guest...﴾ (78). The word "dayf" (ضيف) (2), as we know, came here in the singular, but it is also applied to the plural and the dual, and it serves to indicate the masculine and the feminine as well: if one guest comes you say "hadha dayfi" (this is my guest); if two come you say "hadhani dayfi" (these two are my guests); if a woman, you say "hadhihi dayfi"; if two women, you say "hatani dayfi"; and if a group comes, you say "ha'ulai dayfi" (3).

The Almighty says: ﴿Has there come to you the story of the honoured guests of Abraham?﴾ (Adh-Dhariyat 24).

There are other words in the language as well, such as the word "tifl" (طفل) (4), which is singular; yet it may be applied to a group, although the word "tifl" also has a plural, "atfal" (أطفال).

And the Almighty says: ﴿And let them not display their adornment except what appears thereof, and let them wrap their headcovers over their chests, and not display their adornment except to their husbands, or their fathers, or the fathers of their husbands, or their sons, or the sons of their husbands (5), or their brothers, or the sons of their brothers, or the sons of their sisters, or their women, or what their right hands possess, or male attendants having no physical desire (6), or children who have not yet attained knowledge of the private aspects of women...﴾ (An-Nur 31).

So the word "tifl" is also used, and a group is meant by it.

Here Lot, peace be upon him, asks his people not to disgrace him (7) regarding his guest. Disgrace (khizy) is exposure, both before oneself and before people.

A person may find his own self cheap and approach an evil deed as long as no one sees him; but if people see it, this is an exposure of him, for disgrace happens before the mass of people, while abasement is when the evil deed remains between him and himself.

Lot, peace be upon him, asks: ﴿...Is there not among you a man of right judgement?﴾ (78): that is, is there not among you a man who has reason, manliness and honour (8), who would prevent this matter?

1 - Nothing shows their intense love for this act and their lack of shame more clearly than their committing it in their assembly, which is their gathering place where they meet to talk and consult. The Almighty says: ﴿Do you indeed approach men and cut off the road, and commit the abomination in your assembly...?﴾ (29, Al-'Ankabut). Among what they used to do in their gatherings also: breaking wind, whistling, pigeon-racing, and mocking travellers. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim], and al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti [6/461].

2 - "Dafa yadifuhu dayfan": he alighted at his place, so he is "da'if," and the passive participle is "mudayyaf." "Dayf" is a verbal noun used as an adjective in its own form, so it is not made dual, plural or feminine; though it may be pluralised as "duyuf" and "dayfan." The Almighty says: ﴿He said: "Indeed these are my guests, so do not disgrace me..."﴾ (68, Al-Hijr), meaning: these are my guests, so do not disgrace me by assaulting them. "Dayf" here is in the singular form, while it refers to a number of angels. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim].

3 - The Lord of Majesty, glory be to Him, says: ﴿He said: "Indeed these are my guests, so do not disgrace me..."﴾ (68, Al-Hijr).

4 - "Tifl" (with a kasra on the ta') is the small of anything, and the child of a human being while he is young; it is used for the singular and otherwise alike. The plural occurs in the Almighty's saying: ﴿or children who have not yet attained knowledge of the private aspects of women...﴾ (31, An-Nur), meaning "atfal" (children); and His saying: ﴿Then We bring you forth as children...﴾ (5, Al-Hajj), meaning children. The plural of "tifl" is "atfal," and it occurs in the Qur'an: ﴿And when the children among you reach puberty, let them seek permission...﴾ (59, An-Nur). [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/403], with adaptation.

5 - "Bu'ulatihinna": their husbands.

6 - "Al-irb": a need that requires a stratagem to attain; likewise "al-arba" and "al-ma'rib." The Almighty says: ﴿...or male attendants having no physical desire...﴾ (31, An-Nur), meaning those who have no need of women, i.e. those who have no desire because of their old age, their impotence or their youth. And His saying: ﴿...and I have in it other uses (ma'arib)﴾ (18, Ta-Ha), meaning many other needs and purposes, such as warding off harm or otherwise.

7 - "Akhza'ahu fulan": he humiliated him and disgraced him. The Almighty says: ﴿Our Lord, whomever You cause to enter the Fire, You have indeed disgraced him...﴾ (192, Al 'Imran). Among the supplications of the Qur'an: ﴿And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected﴾ (87, Ash-Shu'ara'). And the Almighty says: ﴿So fear Allah and do not disgrace me concerning my guest...﴾ (78, Hud), meaning: do not humiliate me or expose me by humiliating my guest. The ya' of the first person was dropped from the word "takhzunni" both in writing and pronunciation, for lightness. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/192].

8 - Among the meanings of "rushd" is also that one be firm, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and that he be righteous, reforming, guiding, upright, rightly guided and wise. See the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi [4/3396].

They say: "You certainly know that we have no claim on your daughters, and you certainly know what we want."

This verse contains the reply of those who were pressing their demand for indecency from Lot's people. They said to him: "You know our purpose, and we have no need of your daughters that we would regard as the goal of our coming."

This meant turning away from accepting his advice to them to marry his daughters instead of seeking to commit the immorality with Lot's guests, who were the angels that came in the form of men of perfect beauty.

(1) Scholars differ over what is meant by "daughters": were they truly Lot's own daughters from his loins, or is what is meant the women of his people, since the Prophet is a father to his community, both women and men? See Tafsir Ibn Kathir (2/453), al-Qurtubi (4/3395), and al-Durr al-Manthur of al-Suyuti (4/457).

(2) Ibn Kathir said: "That is: you know that our women have no need for us, and we have no desire for them." Al-Qurtubi also mentioned in his tafsir (4/3397): "The people of Lot had proposed marriage to his daughters, and he rejected them, and it was their custom that whoever was refused in a marriage proposal to a woman could never marry her thereafter."

Then Allah, glory be to Him, sends the reply to Lot, peace be upon him:

﴿He said, "If only I had against you some power, or could take refuge in a strong support."﴾ (80)

When you read the word "law" (لو), this is wishing (تمنّي), that is, hoping that he had a power by which he could repel these people. There must be a condition, as when we say, "If Zayd were with you, I would have come," but here we find a condition without an answer, as if one said, "If I had against you some power, I would have done such and such."

For this reason it is said that the angels told him, "Indeed your support is strong," and therefore he said: ﴿...or could take refuge in a strong support﴾ [Hud]. The strong thing is that which is gathered together in a manner that is difficult to separate, or mixed in a way of blending that is difficult to dissolve. When you gather things, either you gather things whose kinds remain separate but you bind them together firmly, like binding the crucified man to a tree with a strong rope; yet both of them, the crucified man and the tree, remain separate from each other and each has its own essence. There is also what is called khalt (خلط, mixing) and there is what is called mazj (مزج, blending). Khalt is when you mix things, each of which remains distinct from the others so that you can separate it; as for mazj, the blended things cannot be separated from one another.

An example of this: you may mix, for instance, tadmis beans with some peanuts, and you can separate the two from each other, because you combined them while each remained independent. But if you squeeze lemon into a glass of water sweetened with sugar, this is a blend that is difficult to undo.

Lot, peace be upon him, said this because he had no protection from his people, the people of Sodom (Sadum). It is said that it was five villages near Homs.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was amazed at Lot's words, and he said, as narrated by al-Bukhari: "May Allah have mercy on my brother Lot; he used to take refuge in a strong support."

Because of the terror of the sudden calamity that Lot, peace be upon him, suffered, he said that, while he knew that there is no support or refuge stronger than Allah, glory be to Him and exalted.

1 - Awa al-makan: and awa ilayhi yau'wi awyan, he lodged there and sought refuge in it. Allah says: ﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave...﴾ [al-Kahf] meaning they lodged in it and sought refuge in it. (Al-Qamus al-Qawim.)
2 - Rukn al-shay': its strongest side. Allah's words ﴿...or could take refuge in a strong support﴾ [Hud] mean: I seek refuge in a strong fortress that protects me, or in a strong man who protects and supports me against you, as if he were an inaccessible, fortified corner. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/276].
3 - Cited by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur (4/459), attributing it to Ibn Jarir al-Tabari from Wahb ibn Munabbih. Its "strong support" here is Allah, glory be to Him and exalted.
4 - Narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih (3375, 4694), Ahmad in his Musnad (2/326, 332, 350), and Ibn Majah in his Sunan (4026), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 11, verse 81:

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says, recounting what the angels said to Lut (peace be upon him):

﴿They said: "O Lut, we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So travel with your family in a part of the night, and let none of you look back, except your wife; indeed, what strikes them will strike her too. Their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?"﴾

Thus Lut learned, for the first time, that they were messengers of Allah, Exalted is He, although when they spoke with Ibrahim they had not said that they were messengers of Allah. This is to show us that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) knew that they were messengers of the Truth, glorified is He, but he did not know the reason for their coming.

When they informed Lut, "Indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you..." (81), it follows all the more that they would not reach them [his guests]. The angels told Lut to travel with his family by night, that is: go out with your family in a portion of the night. The angels made clear that the appointed time for the punishment (nakal) of the people of Lut is the morning: "...Indeed their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?" (81) [Hud].

Therefore they said: "So travel with your family in a part of the night..." (81) [Hud]. What is intended is that he should leave aside the first quarter of the night and its last quarter, and travel during the middle half of the night, which lies after the first quarter and ends at the last quarter. It has been said that the most fitting meaning of qit' (a part) is the half.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, says: "And let none of you look back..." (81) [Hud]. Al-iltifat (turning/looking back) is turning away from a thing that is before you; it is called turning away from what is facing you. So is the intended meaning the physical turning or the figurative turning?

We know that Lut would take the believers with him, away from their homes, their wealth, and the station and life to which they were accustomed. Therefore the angels warn them not to let their hearts turn toward what they have left behind, and that they must save themselves, and Allah, glorified is He, will compensate them with something better than what they have lost.

This is what is meant by not looking back in the figurative sense, and it is also meant in the physical sense.

The angels instructed Lut (peace be upon him) not to take his wife with him, because she betrayed him by allying herself with the corrupt people and disclosing secrets; he was to leave her with those who would be struck by the punishment.

But at the moment of departure she claimed to be sincere toward Lut and said: "I will go out wherever you go." Then she looked at the people and said: "Woe to my people!" and turned back to remain with them, so that the punishment that befell them would also befall her, at the appointed time the angels had set, which was the morning: "...Indeed their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?" (81) [Hud]. The morning was fixed for their destruction because it is the time of rest and calm, so the punishment is more severe in its chastisement.

Note 1: Qit' and qit'ah: the cut-off portion. Allah, the Exalted, says: "So travel with your family in a part of the night..." (81) [Hud]. Qit' is the plural of "qit'ah." And His saying: "As if their faces had been covered with pieces of the night, dark..." (27) [Yunus]: qit'an, with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ta', and muzlimān is a state (hal) of al-layl. It has also been read qit'an, with a kasra on the qaf and a sukun on the ta', meaning a portion; on this reading, muzlimān is parsed either as an adjective (na't) of qit'an or as a state of al-layl. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/125].

Note 2: Al-nakal: punishment and severe deterrent chastisement. Allah, the Exalted, says: "So Allah seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the first [life]" (25) [al-Nazi'at], meaning Allah punished him with a severe punishment that serves as a lesson to others in this world and the Hereafter. And His saying: "So We made it an exemplary punishment (nakal) for what was before it and what came after it, and an admonition to the God-fearing" (66) [al-Baqarah], meaning Allah made it, through severe punishment, a lesson for the people of its time, for those who came after it, and for the God-fearing in every age. And He, the Exalted, says: "As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, an exemplary punishment (nakalan) from Allah..." (38) [al-Ma'idah], meaning a deterrent penalty imposed by Allah so that people may take warning from it. [al-Qamus al-Qawim].

Note 3: Iltafata al-rajul: he inclined his head and looked to the right or left, or he turned aside and returned from his direction. Allah, the Exalted, says: "So travel with your family in a part of the night, and let none of you look back" (81) [Hud], meaning he should not look to the right or left, nor backward, lest he turn back and withdraw from journeying with you. [al-Qamus al-Qawim 2/196].

Note 4: Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (4/3400): "It is possible that the morning was made the appointed time for their destruction, because souls are most at rest in it, and people are most gathered in it."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 11, verse 82:

The Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿So when Our command came, We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon it stones of hardened clay, layered one upon another, (82)﴾:

Here the Truth, glory be to Him, explains to us that when the command to punishment is issued, the one commanded complies by compulsion. It is said that the towns of the people of Lot were five: the town of "Sodom" (Sadum), the town of "Dadoma", the town of "Da'wa", the town of "Amora", and the town of "Qatam".

His words, exalted is He, ﴿We made its highest part its lowest..(82)﴾ [Hud]: that is, it was overturned completely.

The Qur'an says in another place: ﴿And the overturned cities (al-mu'tafikah) He hurled down (53)﴾ [An-Najm]. Al-mu'tafikah comes from al-ifk, which is deliberate lying, that is, a verbal statement that contradicts reality. Because the one who tells a lie only turns the truth into what is not the truth in his claim, and turns what is not the truth into something resembling the truth.

Likewise al-mu'tafikah, that is, the towns whose highest part was made their lowest, so that their circumstances were overturned.

The command of God was carried out by raining upon them stones of hardened clay, layered, which is clay that has become hardened.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says in another verse: ﴿...stones of clay (33)﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat].

The word "stones" gives a sense of hardness, while the word "clay" gives a sense of softness; but the clay that descended had hardened by God's command, and it descended layered, that is, following one another in order, as if each stone knew its target. For the Truth, glory be to Him, says after that:

﴿Marked by your Lord; and they are not far from the wrongdoers (83)﴾:

1 - Sijjil: hardened clay. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿...and We rained upon it stones of sijjil, layered (82)﴾ [Hud]. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/304].
2 - Al-Qurtubi mentioned in his tafsir (4/3400) "that Gabriel, peace be upon him, inserted his wing beneath the towns of the people of Lot, lifted them from the depths of the earth until he brought them near to the heaven with what was in them, so that the people of heaven heard the braying of their donkeys and the crowing of their roosters; no jar of theirs was overturned, and no vessel of theirs was broken. Then they were turned upside down, and God followed them with stones."
3 - Al-mu'tafikah: the towns overturned when they were sunk. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the companions of Madyan and the overturned cities (70)﴾ [At-Tawbah]; they are the sunken ones, and they are the towns of the people of Lot, whose highest part God made their lowest; they are the mu'tafikah. ﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down (53)﴾ [An-Najm], that is, He toppled them and sank them. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim].
4 - Al-ifk: lying; and Affak is an intensive form, meaning one who lies much. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The devils descend upon every lying sinner (222)﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara]. And He said of the magicians of Pharaoh: ﴿...and behold, it swallows up what they fabricate (117)﴾ [Al-A'raf], that is, what they lie about and claim to be true. This indicates that magic is imagination and deception, not a reversal of the realities of things: the rope is a rope and the serpent is a serpent, but the magician makes people believe he has done something when he has done nothing. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim].
5 - This too concerned the people of Lot. God, exalted is He, said of what Abraham, peace be upon him, said to the angels sent to him: ﴿He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?" (31) They said, "We have been sent to a criminal people (32) to send upon them stones of clay (33) marked by your Lord for the transgressors (34)"﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (*Tafsir al-Sha'rawi*, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 11, verse 83 (part 1 of 2):

The word "*musawwamah*" means "marked," as if each stone had been directed at its particular target. This stone goes to so-and-so, and that one to someone else, like guided missiles aimed at cities. But the precision of these stones is that each one knows exactly on whom it will descend the punishment. God, glorified is He, made them to punish the powerful one (*al-makin*), meaning the human being, and not to destroy the cities.

They are arranged in order, because God, glorified is He, said: ﴿...stones of baked clay, layered﴾ [Hud 82]. The word *sijjil* also occurs in His words: ﴿...birds in flocks, pelting them with stones of baked clay﴾ [al-Fil 3–4].

God, glorified is He, concludes the verse with His words: ﴿...and it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾ [Hud 83]. The "wrongdoers" here means those who disbelieve in the message of God, exalted is He, which followed one another in the procession of the messengers, whose seal is Muhammad (ﷺ).

We know that the Qur'anic narratives were revealed as consolation and steadfastness for the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and as a reminder of the model to follow: ﴿And all that We relate to you of the accounts of the messengers is that by which We strengthen your heart...﴾ [Hud 120].

The narratives recount the battles fought between each messenger, supported by a miracle from God, and those who denied him and disbelieved in him. All these battles ended with the victory of the messenger over the disbelievers. However, the earlier messengers were not charged with fighting for faith. Rather, they were required only to convey the proof of faith and to deliver the method. If the people disobeyed, then heaven itself intervened to chastise the opponents.

God says: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with ʿAd, Iram of the pillars, the like of which was not created in the lands, and Thamud who carved out the rocks in the valley, and Pharaoh of the stakes, who transgressed in the lands and multiplied corruption therein? So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment. Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [al-Fajr 6–14].

But the matter changed with the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ), because the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) is the religion upon which the Hour will be established, and his people are entrusted with conveying the message of God, exalted is He, as successors to the Messenger (ﷺ).

Every individual of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) who knows a ruling of God, exalted is He, must convey it, because he stands in the place of the Messenger (ﷺ).

God says: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you...﴾ [al-Baqarah 143].

Therefore, every individual of his community (ﷺ) is an extension of the message of Islam. Instead of heaven intervening to chastise the disbelievers, God, glorified is He, permitted the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) to stand against the disbelievers with force. Not to impose faith, for faith cannot be imposed or coerced. You may compel a person in matters that are sensory, but you cannot possess his heart, and God, glorified is He, desires the unseen faith that possesses hearts.

For this reason God, glorified is He, says: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they will not be believers. If We willed, We could send down upon them from the sky a sign, so that their necks would remain humbly subdued to it﴾ [al-Shuʿara 3–4].

Therefore, God, glorified is He, wants hearts that are humbled, not necks that are subdued.
