God says: {A withholder of good, transgressor, in disquieting doubt} (25) [Qaf]. [*al-Qamus al-Qawim*, root r-y-b.]

3. This is in God's saying: {And We sent Moses with Our signs and clear authority (96) to Pharaoh and his establishment, but they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not sound} (97) [Hud].

4. This is God's saying: {And Moses said, "O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds (104), obligated to say nothing about God except the truth. I have come to you with clear evidence from your Lord, so send with me the Children of Israel"} (105) [al-A'raf].

5. *Ma* here is negating, meaning *laysa* (there is not). That is: you have no god other than Him.

6. *Al-da'* (داء): illness, whether apparent or hidden, and defect, whether apparent or hidden. One says: so-and-so is *mayyit al-da'*, meaning he does not bear grudges against one who wrongs him. *Da' al-asad* is fever, *da' al-zaby* is health and vigour, *da' al-muluk* is gout, *da' al-karm* is debt and poverty, *dar al-daraa'ir* is permanent evil, *da' al-batn* is blind sedition, and *da' al-dhi'b* is hunger. The plural is *adwa'*. [*al-Mu'jam al-Wasit*, root d-w-'.] The feminine is also permitted: *da'a* with plural *da'at*, and these are diseases whether material or moral.

7. The Truth says: {He has ordained for you of religion what He enjoined upon Noah and that which We revealed to you and that which We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses and Jesus: that you establish the religion and not be divided therein…} (13) [al-Shura]. Thus the values of the religions were gathered in the final Book sent down upon the final Messenger, to unite humanity upon truth, goodness and peace.

8. The intended meaning of the honoured Shaykh is that the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) is the last of the nations since the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) until the Hour is established, and its messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) is the Seal of the Prophets and Messengers.

9. The unity of the Essence (*tawhid al-dhat*) is the language of the heart in oneness, singling out and abstraction towards God. The Truth says: {Say, "Indeed my prayer and my rites and my living and my dying are for God, Lord of the worlds (162), no partner has He; and this I have been commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims"} (163) [al-An'am]. The Essence has bestowals: whenever you mention Him in unity, you are in continual ascent and deserving of the bestowal of the attributes from God, so you deserve mercy from the Merciful, provision from the Provider, and restoration from the Compeller. Whoever loves the Essence is granted the bestowals of the attributes, and in His Most Beautiful Names is the required provision. [From *Min mafhum al-khawatir*.]

10. This is the word that God, glory be to Him, mentioned here: {Had it not been for a word that had preceded from your Lord, the matter would have been decided between them…} (110) [Hud]. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir (4/3423): "The word: that God, mighty and majestic, decreed to delay them until the Day of Resurrection because He knew the good in that; otherwise the matter would have been decided between them, their term being fixed, by rewarding the believer and punishing the disbeliever."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 11, verse 111 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, glorified is He, says:
﴿And indeed, to each of them your Lord will surely pay in full for their deeds. Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do. (111)﴾

So Allah, glorified is He, seized the peoples of the messengers who came before Musa with punishment. As for the beginning of Musa's mission, the punishment was postponed until the Day of Resurrection.

Allah, glorified is He, makes clear: do not think that the postponement of punishment until the Day of Resurrection means escape from punishment. Rather, each person will be paid in full for his deeds: with reward for whoever obeyed, and with punishment for whoever disobeyed. The command of Allah, glorified is He, is coming, without doubt (2). The full payment of recompense is made in proportion to deeds, whether disbelief or faith, righteousness or corruption, and the appointed time for this is the Day of Resurrection.

Here is a pause concerning the style of the Qur'anic text, so that those who do not understand the Arabic language as a natural faculty (3), as the ancient Arabs understood it, may grasp it.

We know that the ancient Arab did not sit with a teacher, yet he understood the language and spoke it correctly, because he belongs to a nation innately (4) endowed with precise and wondrous eloquent expression.

Language, as we know, is neither a race nor blood. Rather, it is a social phenomenon. The society in which a child grows up determines his language. A child who grows up in a society that speaks Arabic will speak Arabic, and a child who lives in a society that speaks English will speak English, because language is what the tongue utters according to what the ear hears.

The majority of the Arab environment in ancient times was an isolated environment, and whoever grew up in it spoke correct language.

As for the Arab who lived in a metropolitan center such as Makkah, Makkah, with its standing, used to receive many foreigners. For this reason, the people of Makkah would take their infants to the desert, so that they would hear nothing but pure classical Arabic, and so that they would not need someone to correct their tongue to the pure language of the Arabs.

To bring this matter closer, let us observe that in our life today there are two languages. One is the language we learn in homes and streets and use in speaking, called "the colloquial language" (al-'amiyya). The other is the language we learn in schools, the refined language distinguished by eloquence and correctness.

The people of Makkah used to send their sons to the desert so that the ear would pick up eloquence (5). The classical language was the "colloquial" of the desert, and a child in the desert did not need a teacher to learn it, because his ear heard nothing but eloquence.

This was the language in which the people of that time were naturally proficient, as a faculty (6). It differs from the language we acquire now and polish in our schools, which is almost artificial. What then of those who did not learn Arabic earlier, such as the Orientalists, who learn the language in old age?

These people did not possess the purity of the language, so they tried to attack the Qur'an, and some of their fools claimed that there is a grammatical error (lahn) in the Qur'an (7). They said this even though they learned the artificial language, whereas those who received the Qur'an from the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, were people of eloquence, and they found no error in the Qur'an. Had they found an error in the Qur'an at the time of its revelation, they would have announced it, because the Qur'an was revealed in the classical language to a nation that was eloquent, articulate, and whose craft was speech.

For some reason, Allah, glorified is He, left the chiefs (8) of Quraysh and the chiefs of the Arabs in their disbelief for a period. Had any of them discovered an error in the Qur'an, he would have announced it.

This is so that no one would say that they believed and then concealed the Qur'an's faults. Had one of them had a flaw to point out, his disbelief would not have prevented him from making it known. So can these Orientalists, who lived in the twentieth century, find an error in the Qur'an, when they did not possess mastery of the language as a faculty, but learned it as a craft, and craft lacks the sense of taste?

An example of this is these people's failure to understand the secrets of the language in the verse about which we are reflecting. Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿And indeed, to each of them your Lord will surely pay in full for their deeds (9). Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do.﴾ That is, each one of those who believed and those who denied will receive full recompense: reward for the obedient, and punishment for the disobedient.

The word "inna", as we know, is in the language a particle of emphasis (tawkid), in response to one who denies what follows it.

Denial, as we know, has stages. If you want to inform someone of news he does not know, you say to him, for example: "So-and-so visited me yesterday."

Thus the news meets the listener's empty mind. If he says to you, "But so-and-so was in another place yesterday," then you say to him, "Indeed, so-and-so visited me yesterday."

If the listener replies to you, "But I met the person you are talking about yesterday in such-and-such a place,"

then here you may reinforce your statement: "By Allah, so-and-so did visit me yesterday."

Thus you bring emphasis in proportion to the degree of denial (10).

When Allah, glorified is He, postpones punishment for some people in this world, a heedless person may say: "Perhaps Allah no longer punishes anyone."

For this reason Allah, glorified is He, made clear, with emphasis, that the reckoning is coming for both the obedient believer and the disobedient denier, and so He said, glorified is He: ﴿And indeed, to each of them your Lord will surely pay in full for their deeds.. (111)﴾

Those who have not attained mastery of the language as a faculty, such as the Orientalists, who took it as a craft, stopped at this verse and said: Why did He use tanwin (11) in the word "kullan" (each)?

They did not know that tanwin stands in place of a whole clause. Whenever you hear or read tanwin, know that it substitutes for a sentence, as in the words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿Why then, when it (the soul) reaches the throat (12), (83) while you are looking on, (84)﴾ In the verse we are reflecting upon, "kullan" summarizes that each of the obedient believer and the disobedient disbeliever will receive his recompense, reward or punishment.

As for His words, glorified is He, ﴿lamma⁠﴾ in the same verse, we know that "lamma" is used in the language in the sense of "when" and "time," as in the words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿And when Musa came at Our appointed time (13), and his Lord spoke to him.. (143)﴾

And as His words, glorified is He: ﴿And when the caravan departed (14), their father said: "Indeed, I find the scent of Yusuf (15).." (94)﴾ That is: when the caravan departed from Egypt, their father said: ﴿Indeed, I find the scent of Yusuf.. (94)﴾

"Lamma" also comes for negation, as in His words, glorified is He: ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts.." (14)﴾ That is: faith has not entered their hearts up to now, and the word "lamma" carries the implication that faith will enter their hearts afterward.

When the word "lamma" is used for negation, it is a particle, like the word "lam," but it differs from "lam," because "lam" apocopates (jazm) the imperfect verb, and its negation is not tied to the moment of speech, but to the past, and circumstances may change. As for "lamma," its negation extends to the time of speaking, and it carries the indication that what it negates will happen. Thus we understand that the words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿And indeed, to each of them your Lord will surely pay in full for their deeds. Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do (16). (111)﴾ mean: each of the obedient and the disobedient will be paid his reckoning and recompense, reward or punishment, when the appointed time of full payment comes, which is the Day of Resurrection.

"Lamma" has come to serve the idea of punishment that used to come in this world, but Allah, glorified is He, willed to postpone punishment for the disbelievers until the Hereafter, and the most fitting particle to express that is "lamma."

When you read ﴿la-yuwaffiyannahum⁠﴾ (surely pay them in full), you find the lam, which is the lam of oath, meaning that Allah, glorified is He, will surely pay them their reckoning, whether reward or punishment.

Allah, glorified is He, is Acquainted with what His servants do. He knows the actions of the servant before they occur, but once they occur they cannot be forgotten or scattered to the winds, because the One who knows them is "al-Khabir" (the Acquainted), the possessor of precise knowledge. The Acquainted differs from the knower who may know generalities, for the Acquainted is one trained in specialization.

For this reason the two words "al-Latif and al-Khabir" often come together, because al-Khabir is the one who knows the places of things, and al-Latif is the one who knows how to reach those places.

An example of this: you may know where a man is hiding in a mountain, for instance. This knowledge and experience are not enough to reach him and penetrate to his place. Rather, this requires more, namely precision and subtlety.

Allah, glorified is He, brought this account about Musa, peace be upon him, to console His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, because some of the disbelievers in Muhammad's message, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Since Allah sends punishment to destroy those who deny His messengers, why does He not bring punishment upon us?"

Therefore this was revealed to inform them that Allah, glorified is He, will surely inflict punishment upon the disbelievers, without doubt. So beware, O Messenger of Allah, lest they deceive you about anything or bargain with you over anything, just as they said: "We worship your god for a year, and you worship our gods for a year (18)."

Allah, glorified is He, had already settled this matter by revealing: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers! (1) I do not worship what you worship (2), nor do you worship what I worship (3), nor will I worship what you have worshipped (4).﴾ This is complete severance of relations in that matter which admits of no bargaining, namely worship.

We know that worship is a matter of the heart, which cannot be bargained over, and severing relations in such a matter is obligatory, because it cannot be negotiated. It is not a relationship of political circumstance, but a divine matter governed by Allah, glorified is He, alone.

The words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿Say, "O disbelievers! (1) I do not worship what you worship (2), nor do you worship what I worship (3), nor will I worship what you have worshipped (4).﴾ This noble statement makes the one who hears and recites it feel that they will continue to worship other than Allah, that Muhammad will continue to worship Allah, and that the word "Allah" will prevail. This is because after Surat al-Kafirun, Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿When the victory of Allah and the conquest come (1), and you see people entering the religion of Allah in multitudes (2), then exalt with the praise of your Lord and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance. (3)﴾

Here Allah, glorified is He, says:
﴿So remain steadfast as you have been commanded, and [so too should] those who have turned back with you [in repentance], and do not transgress. Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do. (112)﴾

1 - Al-Khabir: one of Allah's Beautiful Names. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿...And He is the Wise, the Acquainted (18)﴾ [al-An'am]. Al-Khabir means the Knower of hidden matters. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿...then ask about Him one who is acquainted (59)﴾ [al-Furqan]. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, root kh-b-r].

2 - Al-muhal: what necessitates corruption from every aspect, such as the combination of motion and rest in one body. What is impossible (muhal) among things is that whose existence is not possible. Among speech, muhal is that which is turned away from its proper meaning. Al-mahala means trickery, and its plural is mahal; and mahawil (with fatha on the mim in both). It is said: "There is no mahal in that," meaning: there is no escape from it. [Al-Mu'jam al-Wasit, root h-w-l, adapted].

3 - Al-malaka (with fatha on the mim, lam, and kaf): a firmly established quality in the soul, or a special mental readiness for handling specific tasks with skill and dexterity, such as numerical faculty and linguistic faculty. [Al-Mu'jam al-Wasit, root m-l-k].

4 - Fatara al-shay' fatran: he split it. Its plural is futur, and the noun is fitra. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿The nature of Allah upon which He created mankind (30)﴾ [al-Rum], meaning the creation upon which He created people. And His words, the Exalted: ﴿...Do you see any flaw (3)﴾ [al-Mulk], meaning: any cracks. The interrogation here is for negation, meaning you see no defect at all. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, root f-t-r].

5 - Al-masqul: a passive participle from the verb "saqala": saqala al-shay' saqlan and saqalan, he polished it. It is said: he polished the sword and the mirror and similar things. It is said: he polished his speech, meaning he refined and embellished it. He polished the animal, meaning he trained it. This word is also used to express excelling in something, such as language and talent. It is said: he polished his language, meaning he trained in it until he excelled. He polished his talent through study, meaning he trained in using it until he excelled. [Al-Mu'jam al-Wasit, root s-q-l, adapted].

6 - What shows that the Arabic language in the Arabian Peninsula accompanied sound nature and firmly established faculty is what is related: a water-carrier ordered his son to hold the mouth of a water skin. The boy said to his father: "Father, the skin has overpowered me. Hold its mouth; I have no strength for its back." In this statement are rules for the declension of the five or six nouns: they are inflected with waw in the nominative, with alif in the accusative, and with ya' in the genitive. Examples are countless, and the references contain more for whoever wishes. [Note: the example given is "abati" and "fāhā" as cited in the source].

7 - Lahana li-fulan yalhanu lahnan: he spoke to him in words he understood alone, due to ambiguity, allusion, or hidden indication. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And you will surely recognize them by the tone of their speech (30)﴾ [Muhammad], meaning: you will recognize the hypocrites by their manner of speech, by its concealment and distortion; that is, you will recognize them by errors in speech and slips of the tongue. "Lahana fi kalamihi" means he erred. In the Mu'jam al-Wasit: lahn al-qawl means its meaning, what the attentive listener understands from behind its wording, and it may be explained this way too. The meaning of lahn in language is error in it and departure from its rules. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, root l-h-n, adapted].

8 - Al-sinadid: the strong. Its plural is sanadid. It is said: a hot day with intense heat (yawm hami al-sanadid). It is said: a cold wind, a stormy wind, a rain, meaning intense. The sanadid of fate are its calamities. [Al-Mu'jam al-Wasit, root s-n-d-d, adapted].

9 - Wafa al-shay' yafi wafyan: it was complete and nothing was lost from it. Wafa al-rajul bi-l-'ahd wafa'an: he fulfilled it and carried it out, so he is wafin. The comparative is awfa. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿...And who is more faithful to his covenant than Allah? (111)﴾ [al-Tawba], meaning Allah is greater in fulfillment than anyone else. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Then he will be recompensed with the fullest recompense (41)﴾ [al-Najm], meaning the most complete and perfect recompense. Wafa ilayhi haqqahu: he delivered his right to him in full. This verb takes two objects, so one says: wafahu haqqahu. The active participle is muwaff, a defective noun. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿...Indeed, We will surely give them their share undiminished (109)﴾ [Hud]. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, root w-f-y].

10 - Emphasis for one who denies is among the arts of rhetoric. The Imam al-Suyuti says in al-Itqan [3/193]: "Emphasis varies according to the strength and weakness of the denial, as in His words, the Exalted, recounting the messengers of Jesus when they were denied the first time: ﴿Indeed, we are sent to you (14)﴾ [Ya-Sin], which was emphasized with inna and the nominal sentence. The second time: ﴿They said, 'Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you (16)﴾ [Ya-Sin], which was emphasized with an oath, inna, lam, and the nominal sentence, to match the intensity of the addressees' denial, when they said: ﴿You are not but men like us, and the Most Merciful has sent down nothing; you are only lying (15)﴾ [Ya-Sin]."

11 - Tanwin in language: a silent nun that follows the last letter of a noun in pronunciation and is separated from it in writing. It has several types, among them tanwin of tamkin (fixing), of tankir (indefiniteness), of 'iwad (substitution), and of tarannum (melodic chant). [See Sharh al-Ashmuni 'ala al-Alfiyya, 1/18].

12 - Al-halqum: the throat. Scientifically today, the halqum is a cavity behind the mouth cavity, and it has six openings: the opening of the mouth, the two nostrils, the two ears, and the opening of the larynx. Food and drink pass through the halqum to the person, while the soul passes from the halqum to the larynx. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Then why, when it reaches the throat (83)﴾ [al-Waqi'a], a metaphor for approaching death, meaning: the soul has reached the throat as it leaves the body. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, root h-l-q].

13 - Al-miqat: the specified time for a certain action. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿So the appointed time of his Lord was completed, forty nights (142)﴾ [al-A'raf], meaning the specified time for his Lord's conversation was completed. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is their appointed time, all of them (40)﴾ [al-Dukhan], meaning their specified time for resurrection and reckoning. The plural is mawaqit. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, root w-q-t].

14 - Fasala 'an al-makan: he passed beyond it. He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And when the caravan departed (94)﴾ [Yusuf], meaning it left and went beyond the city. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, root f-s-l].

15 - His words: ﴿Indeed, I find the scent of Yusuf (94)﴾ [Yusuf], meaning a breeze carrying his fragrance, or "wind" in the sense of "scent," that is, his fragrance. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, vol. 1, p. 280].

16. Al-Khabir (the All-Aware): one of God's Beautiful Names (al-asma' al-husna). God Most High says: "...and He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware" [al-An'am]. Khabar, in the sense of knowing a matter (khabar al-amr), is like 'ilm (knowledge), and 'alima bihi (he knew of it). Both forms, in wording and meaning, mean that he is khabir with it. Al-Khabir is the one who knows the inner aspects of matters. God Most High says: "...so ask about Him one who is well-informed" [al-Furqan]. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, root kh-b-r].

17. God's promise has its appointed time, which He intends. This confirms His saying: "And do not think that God is unaware of what the wrongdoers do. He only defers them to a Day when eyes will stare" [Ibrahim], and His saying: "We will draw them gradually [toward destruction] from where they do not perceive. And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm" [al-Qalam].

18. Al-Wahidi mentions in Asbab al-Nuzul (Occasions of Revelation) [p. 261] that "a group of Quraysh said: 'O Muhammad, come, follow our religion and we will follow yours. You worship our gods for a year, and we will worship your God for a year. If what you have brought is better than what is in our hands, we will have shared in it and taken our portion of it. And if what is in our hands is better than what is in your hand, you will have shared in our affair and taken your portion.' He said: 'God forbid that I associate anything else with Him.' So God revealed: 'Say: O disbelievers' [al-Kafirun] to the end of the surah. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out to the Sacred Mosque, where the chiefs of Quraysh were, and recited it to them until he finished the surah. At that, they despaired of him."

19. God Most High says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): "When God's help comes, O Muhammad, against your people of Quraysh, and the conquest" — the conquest being the conquest of Mecca — "and you see people from the various kinds and tribes of the Arabs entering the religion of God in multitudes" — that is, into the religion of God with which He sent you — "in multitudes": i.e., in groups, one group after another. "So glorify your Lord with His praise": i.e., glorify your Lord and magnify Him with His praise and thanks. "And seek His forgiveness": ask Him to forgive your sins. "Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance": i.e., He returns to His obedient servant with what He loves. [Mukhtasar Tafsir al-Tabari, adapted].

20. Istaqama al-shay' (the thing became straight): it became free of crookedness. Istaqama al-mu'min (the believer became upright): he followed the straight path. God Most High says: "So as long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them..." [al-Tawbah], i.e., keep faithful to your covenant with them for as long as they keep theirs, and do not break the covenant with you. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, root q-w-m].

21. Taghā yatghū taghwānan wa-taghwā is a waw-verb (hollow verb with waw), meaning: to exceed the limit in oppression and aggression. Taghā yatghā taghyānan is a ya'-verb (with ya'), meaning: to exceed the limit. God Most High says: "Who transgressed in the lands" [al-Fajr], i.e., they wronged and exceeded the limit in disobedience. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, root t-gh-y].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 11, verse 112:

Istiqamah (steadfastness, uprightness) means the absence of inclination or deviation, even to the width of a hair. This is something difficult to achieve, because the dividing line between two opposites, or between two contradictory things, is sometimes finer than a hair.

An example of this: when you see shadow and light, at times the shadow climbs over the light, and at times the light climbs over the shadow. We will find it difficult to determine the dividing line between shadow and light, however precise the measures.

Thus separating a thing from its opposite becomes difficult, and therefore istiqamah is an extremely arduous matter.

When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hud and its sisters have made me grey-haired."

Were it not that the Truthful One, glory be to Him, said in His Noble Book: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [At-Taghabun] (16).

Had this verse not been revealed, the Muslims would have been utterly exhausted. Allah, glory be to Him, revealed this statement after He had said: ﴿Fear Allah with the fear due to Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran] (102), and this was hard on the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so the Truthful One, glory be to Him, revealed what would lighten the burden on the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), saying, glory be to Him: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [At-Taghabun] (16).

So then: the command to istiqamah is a command to precision in carrying out what is required of Allah, in commands and prohibitions, such that we do not incline toward one side rather than another.

Thus istiqamah demands complete alertness and the absence of heedlessness.

The Truthful One says: ﴿So remain steadfast as you have been commanded, and [so too] those who turned back with you﴾ [Hud] (112). This is a notice that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) should not despair at the stand of the chieftains of Quraysh against his call (ﷺ), because they would fall away day after day.

And the saying of the Truthful One: ﴿...and do not transgress. Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do﴾ [Hud] (112). It means: that we do not exceed the limit, for transgression (tughyan) is going beyond the limit.

Thus we know that faith has set a limit for everything, except that the limits of commands differ from the limits of prohibitions. If the Truthful One commands you to something, He requires you to adhere to it and not to exceed it.

The Truthful One said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ [Al-Baqarah] (229). This statement concerns commands. As for prohibitions, He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them﴾ [Al-Baqarah] (187), meaning: that you keep entirely away from them.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever falls into doubtful matters falls into the forbidden, like the shepherd who grazes around the sanctuary (hima), who is about to graze within it. Verily, every king has a sanctuary, and the sanctuary of Allah is His prohibitions."

When the Truthful One forbids us to approach something, this is the istiqamah of caution (ihtiyat), and it may cause you to bring into the prohibition what is not part of it. For example, when wine was prohibited, the command came to avoid it, meaning keeping away from everything connected with wine, so that the Muslim and wine do not come together in one place.

The Truthful One also made istiqamah a matter of obedience, and He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And give its due on the day of its harvest, and do not be excessive﴾ [Al-An'am] (141). The prohibition of excess here is so that the Truthful One protects us from a moment in which we remember how much we have harvested, yet we find nothing with which to sustain our necessity (awad). A person may be lavish at the moment of harvest because of how much he has, then difficult circumstances come upon him and he says: "Would that I had not given!" Thus the Truthful One protects us from this situation.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Be upright (sadidu) and be moderate (qaribu). Know that none of you will enter Paradise by his deeds, and that the most beloved of deeds to Allah is the most constant of them, even if it is little." Because religion is strong and firm, and "no one overburdens himself in religion except that it overcomes him."

Thus we find that the Truthful One and His Messenger (ﷺ) know us best. Allah does not want us to avoid transgression only with regard to prohibited things, but also with regard to what is permitted. So He enjoins upon us gentleness, softness and ease, and that a person leave himself room for choice.

An example: a person binds himself to twenty rak'ahs every night, and he binds himself to this by a vow to Allah in a moment of clarity, but when he begins to practise that amount he discovers its difficulty, and his soul comes to dislike it.

Therefore the Truthful One commands us to istiqamah and to avoid transgression: istiqamah in determining what is commanded and what is forbidden. For this reason, caution in matters of worship is broader for one who seeks istiqamah.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters that many people do not know. Whoever guards against doubtful matters has cleared himself (istabra'a) regarding his religion and his honour."

Therefore the Wise Lawgiver, glory be to Him, asks us in caution sometimes to be cautious by adding, and sometimes by reducing. When you pray outside the Sacred Mosque, it is sufficient that your direction is the Ka'bah. But when you pray in the Sacred Mosque, you know that the Ka'bah has two parts: one part whose building is high, and a part called "al-Hatim" (17), which is part of the Ka'bah, but its expenses in the days of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fell short, so they did not build it (18).

Therefore you direct your gaze toward the high building, whose Ka'bah-ness is certain, and this is caution by reduction.

As for caution by addition, an example of it is tawaf. People may crowd around the Ka'bah, and your circumstances allow only circumambulating around the Mosque.

Thus the tawaf lengthens for you, but it is tawaf with addition. In prayer the caution is by reduction, while in tawaf the caution is by addition.

Thus we find that caution is what defines the meaning of istiqamah.

The Truthful One concludes the verse with His saying: ﴿...Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do﴾ [Hud] (112).

In the preceding verse He said: ﴿...Indeed, He is Aware of what they do﴾ [Hud] (111).

We have known the meaning of Khabir (Aware). As for what is meant by Basir (Seeing) here, it is that He, glory be to Him, knows the movement of worship, because the movement of worship is visible.

1 - From Abu Juhayfah, who said: They said, "O Messenger of Allah, we see you have grown grey?" He said, "Hud and its sisters have made me grey." Recorded by Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah [4/350]. Al-Haythami cited it in al-Majma' [7/37] from the hadith of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir, attributing it to al-Tabarani, and said: "its narrators are the narrators of the Sahih." The sisters of Surah Hud that greyed the Messenger of Allah are Surah al-Waqi'ah, al-Mursalat, al-Naba' and al-Takwir. See al-Tirmidhi in his Sunan [3297].
2 - Ittaqa: its origin is [awtaqa] on the pattern [if'tala]; the waw of the root was changed to ta', and it was assimilated into the ta' of the ifta'ala form. Ittaqa Allah means to avoid what displeases Him and what causes His punishment, by obedience to Allah and by keeping the servant away from His disobedience. The Almighty said: ﴿...la'allakum tattaqun﴾ [Al-Baqarah] (21), i.e., that you guard yourselves from the punishment of Allah by obeying Him and abandoning His disobedience. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim, root w-q-y].
3 - Tuqah: taqwa and guarding oneself; its origin is wiqyah, the waw was changed to ta' and the ya' to alif, and its plural is tuqa. The Almighty said: ﴿illa an tattaqu minhum tuqah...﴾ [Ali 'Imran] (28), i.e., unless you fear from them harm and beware of them something disliked that you would not want for yourselves. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim: root w-q-a].
4 - I'tada: to wrong and transgress. The Almighty said: ﴿fa-man i'tada 'alaykum fa'tadu 'alayhi bi-mithli ma i'tada 'alaykum...﴾ [Al-Baqarah] (194), i.e., punish him for his aggression; the punishment of the aggressor is called i'tida' by way of correspondence. 'Adā ya'dū, 'adwan means to run; 'adā 'alayhi 'adwan wa 'udwanan means to wrong him and attack him, like i'tada 'alayhi. The meaning of not transgressing here is not exceeding the limits of Allah that He has forbidden to commit. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim: root '-d-w, adapted].
5 - Qaraba al-amr, uqribuhu, qurbanan and qurban: to do it or to come near it. From it is the saying of the Almighty: ﴿wa la taqrabu al-zina...﴾ [Al-Isra'] (32), and His saying: ﴿wa la taqraba hadhihi al-shajarah...﴾ [Al-Baqarah] (35), i.e., do not come to it, do not touch it, and do not eat from it. The prohibition in this manner is a fortiori with regard to the thing itself. Likewise: ﴿wa la taqrabu al-zina﴾ [Al-Isra'] (32), where He forbade drawing near to it, which is a prohibition of touching, kissing and the like that bring a person close to falling into it. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim: root q-r-b].
6 - Al-Nawawi said in his commentary: "Its meaning is that the kings among the Arabs and others each have a sanctuary which he protects from the people, preventing them from entering it. Whoever enters it is punished, and whoever is cautious for himself does not come near that sanctuary, out of fear of falling into it." [3/1220], ed. Fu'ad 'Abd al-Baqi.
7 - Al-Rat': eating greedily; al-rat' in fertile land is grazing in it. Arta'a al-qawm: they fell into abundance and grazed. [Lisan al-'Arab: root r-t-'].
8 - Agreed upon: al-Bukhari recorded it in his Sahih [2051] and Muslim in his Sahih [1599], from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir.
9 - Asrafa: exceeded moderation and balance, so it is israf; it occurs in wealth and in other things. The Almighty said: ﴿wa al-ladhina idha anfaqu lam yusrifu wa lam yaqturu wa kana bayna dhalika qawaman﴾ [Al-Furqan] (67), i.e., moderate in spending wealth. He also said: ﴿qul ya 'ibadiya alladhina asrafu 'ala anfusihim la taqnatu min rahmati Allah...﴾ [Al-Zumar] (53), i.e., they exceeded moderation and balance in many matters, multiplying sins against themselves. He said: ﴿fa-la yusrif fi al-qatl...﴾ [Al-Isra'] (33), i.e., let him not kill more than the killer, as they used to do in the Jahiliyyah, killing a noble man in greater number from the killer's tribe. He said: ﴿wa la tuti'u amr al-musrifin﴾ [Al-Shu'ara'] (151). Israf occurs in many matters, not in spending wealth alone. Among the sayings of the righteous: there is no excess in good, and no good in excess. [Al-Qamus al-Qawim: root s-r-f].
10 - Al-awad: that which is the necessary sustenance by which one's life is sustained.
11 - Sadda al-shay' sadadan wa sududan: became upright. It is said: sadda al-sahm (the arrow hit true); sadda fulan: his saying and action hit the mark; sadda qawluhu wa fi'luhu: he became upright and correct. So he is sadid, and al-sadad is uprightness, moderation and what is right in speech and action. [Al-Mu'jam al-Wasit: root s-d-d, adapted].
12 - Agreed upon: recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih [6463] and Muslim in his Sahih [2816], from Abu Hurayrah.
13 - From Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed this religion is firm, so proceed in it gently." Recorded by Ahmad in his Musnad [3/199].
14 - From Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed this religion is ease, and no one overburdens himself in religion except that it overcomes him. So be upright, draw near (to the goal), rejoice, and seek help with the morning, the evening, and a part of the night." Recorded by al-Nasa'i in his Sunan [8/122].
15 - Bayyin: an intensive form of bayan, meaning extremely clear.
16 - Istabra'a from religion and sin: sought to be cleared of it; istabra'a al-shay': searched thoroughly for it in order to remove doubt from it. [Al-Mu'jam al-Wasit: root b-r-'].
17 - Al-Hatim: the wall; here it is the wall of the Ka'bah. Al-Azhari said: it is the one in which the gutter is; it was called hatim because the House was raised and that part was left broken off (mahtum). [Lisan al-'Arab: root h-t-m].
18 - From 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the Jidr (which is the Hijr of the Ka'bah): is it part of the House? He said: "Yes." I said: "Then why did they not include it in the House?" He said: "Your people were short of expenses." I said: "Then what about its door being raised?" He said: "Your people did that so that they could let in whom they wished and prevent whom they wished. Had your people not just recently left disbelief, and had I not feared that their hearts would be troubled, I would have considered adding the Jidr to the House and making its door level with the ground." Agreed upon. Recorded by al-Bukhari in his Sahih [1584] and Muslim in his Sahih [1333, narration no. 10].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 11, verse 113:

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says:

﴿And do not incline toward those who do wrong, lest the Fire touch you, and you would have no protectors other than Allah; then you would not be helped.﴾ (11:113):

The disbelievers, as we know, had proposed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he worship their gods for a year, and that they would worship Allah for a year. But the Truthful, glorified is He, cut off and decided this matter.

Here comes the emphasis on this matter; so He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And do not incline toward those who do wrong..(11:113)﴾ [Hud]. Al-rukun (inclination) is leaning, settling, affection and mercy. When you incline toward the wrongdoer, you give him the impression that his strength has weight in your call.

Al-rukun also means: flattery, helping this wrongdoer in his wrongdoing, and adorning to people what this wrongdoer has done.

The affliction of worldly life is inclining toward wrongdoers, because inclining toward them only encourages them to persist in wrongdoing and to spread it. The lowest degree of inclining toward the wrongdoer is that you do not prevent him from wronging others, and the highest degree of inclining toward the wrongdoer is that you adorn this wrong for him and adorn it for people.

If you survey the state of wrongdoing in the whole world, you will find that the afflictions of human societies arise only from inclining toward the wrongdoer. But when you distance yourself from the wrongdoer and boycott him, you and those with you, he will think that you turned away from him only because you are confident of another, stronger support. So he becomes shaken within himself, reckoning with the strength you rely upon, and in this there is a weakening of his influence, and in this there is isolation and deterrence for him, perhaps he will be restrained from his wrongdoing.

Inclining toward the wrongdoer makes a person liable to be touched by the Fire to the extent of the effects of this inclination, because the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿And do not incline toward those who do wrong, lest the Fire touch you, and you would have no protectors other than Allah; then you would not be helped.﴾ [Hud].

So when you incline toward a wrongdoer, you fall into enmity with the method of Allah, and Allah forsakes you and no one helps you, because there is no protector and no helper except Allah, exalted is He.

1 - Rakana, yarkunu, ruknan and rukunan: he inclined toward it and settled, and rukn of a thing is its strongest side. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿...or I would take refuge in a strong support (11:80)﴾ [Hud], meaning: I would seek a strong fortress that protects me, or a strong man who protects and helps me against you, as if he were an impregnable, secure support. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not incline toward those who do wrong, lest the Fire touch you...(11:113)﴾ [Hud], meaning: do not lean toward them and rely upon them. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And had We not made you firm, you would have almost inclined toward them a little (17:74)﴾ [al-Isra], meaning: you would lean toward them [al-Qamus al-Qawim: entry rakana].
2 - Al-zulm (wrongdoing): transgressing the limit and departing from the truth, or diminishing and reducing it, and it is the opposite of justice. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves (16:118)﴾ [al-Nahl]. Al-zalim (the wrongdoer) is an active participle; the Truthful says: ﴿while he is wronging himself...(18:35)﴾ [al-Kahf]. Al-zallam is an intensive form; the Truthful says: ﴿Indeed, man is greatly unjust and ungrateful (14:34)﴾ [Ibrahim], and zallam is an intensive form; the Truthful says: ﴿And I am not ever unjust to the servants (50:29)﴾ [Qaf]. Mazlum is a passive participle; the Truthful says: ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully...(17:33)﴾ [al-Isra] [al-Qamus al-Qawim 1/416, 417].
3 - Massahu, yamassuhu, massan: he passed his hand over it without a barrier. Massathu al-nar: it reached him, touched his skin, and harmed him. Massahu al-marad (figuratively): it afflicted him. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿...and when harm touches him, he is despairing (17:83)﴾ [al-Isra] [al-Qamus al-Qawim: entry massa].

And Allah, the Exalted, says after that:

﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and in some hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove misdeeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.﴾ (114)

This is a command to good, which Allah directs to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

We notice in these verses of Surah Hud that they contain commands and prohibitions: the commands are always to good, and the prohibitions are always against evil.

We also notice that the Exalted said: ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded, and [so too] those who turned with you...﴾ (112) [Hud]. Then He directed the prohibition to the whole Ummah: ﴿And do not transgress...﴾ (112) [Hud]. He did not say "So be steadfast and do not transgress," because the command to good comes to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Ummah with him, while the prohibition of evil is addressed to the Ummah. In this there is an affirmation of the elevated station of the Prophet (ﷺ).

We see the same matter when the Exalted addresses the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), saying: ﴿And do not incline toward those who have done wrong...﴾ (113) [Hud]. He did not say, "And do not incline toward those who have done wrong" in the singular.

Here, in the verse about which we are reflecting, the Exalted says to His Messenger (ﷺ) and to his Ummah: ﴿Establish the prayer...﴾ (114) [Hud]. Iqamah (establishing) means performing the required act in its most complete form, like "iqamat al-bunyan" (the erecting of a building), and making it fulfil the purpose for which it is intended.

It is said: "aqama al-shay'" meaning he made the thing stand upright on the matter by which it performs its function.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends² of the day...﴾ (114) [Hud]: that is, its end on one side and its end on the other side, because the "tarf" (end) of a thing is its limit.

The limits of the two ends are determined from the middle region of the thing, for the middle is the dividing line between the two ends. What lies to the right of the middle is considered one end, and what lies to the left of the middle is considered the other end; every portion beyond the middle is an end.

Usually the middle is the exact midpoint; what is on its right is divided into ten parts, and what is on its left is divided into ten other parts, and each section between those parts on the right and those on the left is considered an end.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day...﴾ (114) [Hud] requires that you know that we recognize the day from the first light of true dawn. This is the first end, in which we establish the Fajr prayer. Then comes Zuhr. If Zuhr falls before the zawal³, we count it in the region before the middle; if it is after the zawal, we count it in the region after the middle.

After Zuhr there is 'Asr, which is another end.⁴

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And in some hours of the night...﴾ (114) [Hud] requires us to understand that the word ﴿zulfan﴾ is the plural of "zulfah," derived from "azlafahu," meaning he brought him near.

The plural has a minimum of three. We know that for us in the night there are the Maghrib prayer and the 'Isha' prayer. For this reason we find that Imam Abu Hanifa considers the witr⁵ to be obligatory (wajib). He said: the 'Isha' prayer is fard (obligatory), and the witr prayer is wajib; and there is a difference between fard and wajib.⁶

The Exalted says immediately after that: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove misdeeds⁷...﴾ (114) [Hud]. This connecting statement places the prayer at the summit of good deeds, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) clarified this when he said: "The five prayers, and Friday to Friday, are expiation for what is between them, so long as major sins are not committed."⁸

The scholars differed about the meaning of "sayyi'at" (misdeeds) and "hasanat" (good deeds). Some of them said: the good deed is that for whose performance Allah has appointed a reward, and the misdeed is that for whose performance Allah has appointed a punishment.

The first of the good deeds in faith is that you bear witness that there is no god but Allah. This is a good deed that removes disbelief, because good deeds remove misdeeds.

For this reason some scholars said: a Muslim who commits a sin or one of the major sins will not remain eternally in the Fire, because if the good deed of faith has removed the misdeed of disbelief, why would it not remove what is less than disbelief?

Thus the punishment is lightened for the Muslim, so he receives his punishment from the Fire, but he does not remain in it forever, because we cannot equate those who believe in Allah with those who do not believe in Allah.

Faith in Allah is the greatest good deed, and this good deed removes disbelief; and by greater reason it removes what is less than disbelief.

Some scholars asked: are the obligatory acts (fara'id) the good deeds that remove misdeeds?

Some of them answered: There are authentic hadiths that have come from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning good deeds other than obligatory acts. Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) not say that fasting the Day of 'Arafah is expiation from one Arafah to the next Arafah, removing misdeeds?⁹

Did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) not say that the person who receives a blessing of Allah with the words: "All praise is for Allah who provided it to me without any ability (hawl)¹⁰ or power from me, and all praise is for Allah who clothed me without any ability or power from me," this saying erases misdeeds?

Did he (ﷺ) not say that when you say: "Glory be to Allah, and praise be to Allah, and there is no god but Allah, and Allah is greatest, and there is no power nor might except by Allah, the Most High, the Mighty," this saying is an expiation?

So good deeds are absolute, whether they are obligatory or not obligatory, and they remove misdeeds; and a misdeed is an act for whose doing the Exalted has threatened the doer with punishment.

Some scholars also asked: a misdeed is an act, and an act, once it has occurred, is recorded and preserved, so how can a good deed remove it?

They answered: The removal of a misdeed happens either through the one who guards the deed and records it against you, so Allah erases it from the book of your misdeeds; or Allah, the Exalted, pardons you so that He does not punish you for it; or the deed itself is removed, so it is not realized, and what has occurred is not lifted up; or Allah preserves it if it has occurred, because He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Not a word does he utter but that with him is an observer, ready.﴾ (18) [Qaf].

He, the Exalted, also says: ﴿And indeed, over you are watchers, noble and recording.﴾ (10–11) [Al-Infitar].

Thus the removal of a misdeed happens either by its erasure from the record, or it remains in the record and Allah removes its punishment through forgiveness.

The Exalted says: ﴿Those who avoid the major sins and immoralities, except for minor faults. Indeed, your Lord is vast in forgiveness...﴾ (32) [An-Najm]. Avoiding major sins does not prevent the occurrence of minor ones.

The Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, the prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing...﴾ (45) [Al-'Ankabut]. When we look at the appointed times of the prayer, we find them to be five times. Whoever's heart is attached to the prayer, his heart is occupied throughout the time of his movement with establishing the prayer. Then the time of night comes for him to sleep, and everyone who commits a sin will have his thought occupied with it for a period; if the time of prayer had not come to him, he would feel lost. But when the time of prayer comes, his heart turns to Allah, the Exalted, seeking forgiveness.

If the sin has occurred from him once, he may not commit it again, or the prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing at the time of preparing for it. Whoever sits to sleep upon others, or wrongs people, when he hears the call to prayer and rises and performs wudu', he has shown mercy to people during his wudu', during his prayer, and at his conclusion of the prayer.

There are many acts here, from obligatory acts and good deeds, and they erase misdeeds. The Muslim must be occupied with increasing good deeds, and not occupied with erasing misdeeds, because one good deed is rewarded tenfold, and Allah may multiply it; but a misdeed is recorded only as one.

The Exalted concludes this noble verse with His saying: ﴿...That is a reminder for those who remember.﴾ (114) [Hud]. That is: establishing the prayer at the two ends of the day and in some hours of the night are good deeds that remove misdeeds; and in that is a reminder and an alert for the soul to something it had overlooked. That is, this thing was already present before, but heedlessness came to make it forgotten. The first information removed ignorance of this thing, and the second information reminds you of the ruling. The human's failing is that the matters that pass through him, from sights and perceptions, follow one another, and the things that were at the focal point of awareness (bu'rat al-shu'ur)¹¹ move to its periphery (hashiyat al-shu'ur), so the person becomes heedless of what has moved to the periphery of awareness, and there must come a new meaning to remind him of what has gone out of view on the periphery.

An example of this: if you throw a stone into the sea, this stone settles at a focal point that creates circles of water around it, and these circles travel until they disappear from human sight. The proof of this is that you may remember events that passed over you twenty years or more ago; those events were present on the periphery of awareness, and then something came to you that alerted you to them.

The brain, like a photographic camera, sometimes captures an image in one attempt and sometimes in two or more; and the capture from the first time happens because the brain in that moment was free of passing thoughts.

We find that those who have lost their sight are blessed by Allah with another blessing, namely their great ability to retain knowledge; because when the blind person hears knowledge, he is not preoccupied by visible passing thoughts that steal the attention of the focal point of awareness. As for the one who can see, what passes before him may steal the focus of his awareness, so he hears the knowledge more than once until the knowledge meets the focal point of awareness free and settles in it.

This is what reminding does: it summons what is on the periphery of awareness to the focal point of awareness. So if you have been distracted from obedience and gone toward disobedience, reminding shows you the horizons of responsibility that follow disobedience, which is punishment.

For this reason it is said: "There is no good in a good after which is the Fire, and no evil in an evil after which is Paradise."

The Exalted says here, in the verse about which we are reflecting: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day and in some hours of the night...﴾ (114) [Hud].

When you look at the pillars of Islam, you will find that you bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, once in a lifetime. The second pillar, the prayer, is a pillar that never lapses. It is five times every day; in it you utter the testimony, and you purify yourself with part of the time so that Allah, the Exalted, may bless for you what remains of your time; and in it you fast from food and drink and everything that breaks the fast; and at the moment of standing for prayer you turn toward the Sacred House.

In the prayer the other acts of worship become clear, for in it are the five pillars of Islam.

For this reason the prayer never lapses; for if you cannot pray standing, you may pray seated; and if you cannot move, you may move the eyelashes of your eyes while praying.¹²

Thus you find in the prayer all the pillars of the religion. Because of its importance, it remains with the person until the last breath of his life. Its importance in legislation is equal to its importance in obligation. All of Islam's obligations came through revelation, except the prayer, which came directly from Allah, the Exalted; for Allah, the Exalted, summoned His Messenger (ﷺ) to Himself to prescribe the prayer upon him.¹³ It is a gift to the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ), because it was legislated during the closeness of Muhammad (ﷺ) to his Lord, the Exalted.

Therefore Allah, the Exalted, made the prescribed prayer a means of nearness for the entire Ummah of His Messenger (ﷺ); and for this reason it is the one that remains.

It is related that Imam 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face and be pleased with him, came to a people and said: "Which verse in the Book of Allah is most hopeful to you?"

That is: which verse gives hope, reassurance, and good news that Allah, the Exalted, accepts us, forgives us, and has mercy on us? Some of them said: it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills...﴾ (116) [An-Nisa'].

Imam 'Ali said: "A good verse, but not the one."¹⁴ That is, it is a verse that fulfils what he asked, but it is not the verse he meant.

Some of the people said: it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever does wrong or wrongs himself and then seeks forgiveness of Allah will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (110) [An-Nisa'].

Imam 'Ali repeated: "A good verse, but not the one."

Some of the people said: it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins...﴾ (53) [Az-Zumar].

Imam 'Ali said: "A good verse, but not the one."

Then some of them said: it is His saying, the Exalted: {And those who, when they commit an immorality...}
